title: Ignite 2026: Building the frontier ecosystem
body: Ignite 2026: Building the frontier ecosystem Nov 17, 2026 | Microsoft Corporate Blogs Satya Nadella, Microsoft Chairman and CEO, delivered the opening keynote at Ignite in San Francisco this morning. Here is an edited version of his remarks. This week is about two things: First is how we capitalize on new capabilities that are growing exponentially. And second is how do we build the capability to deal with the consequences of these exponentials. At times like these, I always find it helpful to be grounded in our mission: To empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more. In today’s world, that means building a frontier ecosystem. We need to parlay any technological advance into real outcomes and new points of leverage for people, organizations and society at large. For us, that comes down to three things: Keeping human ambition at the center, ensuring your control of your organization’s intelligence and learning, and trust. And so, our goal is to build a stack that addresses these three core architectural principles. Copilot Copilot is the new OS for work. Copilot brings together all the new form factors of human-computer interaction, whether it is Chat, Cowork, Code or Autopilot, into one experience. It also brings together the disparate categories of knowledge work, coding and business process. That is why we have all of Office with its richness built into Copilot. And underlying it is a model system that matches the right intelligence to the right context to the right form factor to accomplish the task. Home gives you one place to start, whether you need a quick answer or want to assign and complete complex, multi-step tasks. Code brings the power of an infinite SaaS factory to every individual. It lets you build your own custom SaaS apps, dashboards and much more. And Autopilot is an autonomous agent that keeps moving your work forward 24×7 in all the places where you and your team collaborate. Underlying all this is Work IQ. You can think of this as the most important database for any organization, with a deep understanding of people, their relationships, documents, emails, meetings, chats and projects that make up the fabric of work. And we are going further. We are extending Copilot for specific roles: sales, legal, finance, service. We are organizing the skills, connectors and plugins for these roles across the entire surface area of Copilot. And that includes third-party systems, too. In fact, today we are announcing new plugins for business applications, starting with Dynamics 365. And it is not just Dynamics. We are very excited to partner with Salesforce to bring Salesforce to Copilot. And we are going beyond that as well. Up until now, we have mostly been in a single player world of people and their agent loops and swarms. But the time has come for a true multiplayer form factor, where people, their agents and other people are all driving towards a common goal, with shared context. This is Copilot Workspaces: YouTube Video Click here to load media Microsoft IQ The idea behind IQ is to help every organization build, retain and continuously improve its own intelligence. Essentially, we are taking the system we built underneath Copilot and externalizing it as a first-class platform that embodies your organizational intelligence as an asset that you continuously build and control. We are bringing together all of the data you have across Fabric, Foundry and Microsoft 365. And, of course, all the third-party context too. Microsoft IQ comes with hundreds of new connectors we are announcing today, so agents can get the full enterprise context where business gets done. And all this rich context manifests as business plugins that can be shared and inherited across the organization. Models For us, it is about mapping intelligence to a given task, with the best economics. This is something we can uniquely do in the context of real-world tasks by tuning our products, harness and tools, and the model system, end-to-end. And today we are thrilled to announce Microsoft-Decision-1.1, which is now generally available and ready for enterprise deployment. We have added multimodal support. And we have improved performance, making decisions more accurate and responses faster. Already, more than 4,000 customers have used it. And we ourselves are using it for core tasks like routing, data labeling, personalization, content filtering and hundreds of other use cases. Foundry of course has all the most popular closed and open weight models, too. We are very excited to bring GPT 6.2 to Foundry. It is a great model that sets a new bar for AI in professional work. And today we are announcing that Meta’s latest models are all coming to Foundry as well. We are also innovating at the frontier with our own MAI model family that is both compute-efficient when it comes to pre-training and token-efficient when it comes to product deployment. Our goal is to put additional points on the frontier curve informed by real world task-performance. And we are going further. We are announcing MAI Licensed Weights, meaning our trusted customers will now be able to get access to Microsoft AI model weights through our Frontier Co. Today, we are introducing lots of new models. But I want to highlight two in particular: First, Code. We are introducing our new flagship family of agentic coding models: Code 2. Code 2 is at the frontier of cost-performance for everyday enterprise coding tasks. It excels in taking code to production, deep debugging, multifile implementation, repo-wide reasoning and UI at a fraction of frontier cost. Code 2 Flash is designed for fast, high-volume work like code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes and rapid iterations. It brings near-flagship quality for a much lower cost. These models are both generally available today on GitHub Copilot, both in the model picker and as part of Copilot Fusion. They are also available in Foundry. We are taking the same approach in cyber. Cyber 2 Flash is our most capable security model yet. It is a flash-sized model that delivers performance ahead of frontier models at a fraction of the cost per task. And, just as we have done with coding, we are co-designing the model with the tools and systems where it will be used. We are integrating Cyber 2 with Perception. Agent 365 Successfully deploying AI systems starts with making sure you have observability at every layer of the stack. That is where Agent 365 comes in. It is a control plane that extends your existing governance, identity, security and management systems to the agents in your enterprise. We already have over 50 million agents in Agent 365. And it includes FinOps, too. As AI scales, every organization needs a clear line between what it spends and the value AI creates. That is why today we are announcing Agent 365 Business Analytics. You can think of it as your ERP system for AI usage. You can see exactly what is driving spend. You can connect spend to outcomes to drive business value. And you can optimize ROI across different scenarios. Security The next thing I want to talk about is how you take the environment you have set up, from Copilot to IQ to Agent 365, and secure it. And that is where Perception and our security stack comes in. We are building an end-to-end trust platform. We are helping customers both secure their AI deployments and use AI to strengthen their security posture. Perception is a complete agentic security system with teams of red, blue and green agents that run through playbooks to deliver security outcomes at machine speed, with you always in control. Essentially, think about it like this: red team agents simulate attacks, blue team agents detect attacks and green team agents fix and remediate. With Playbooks, you can compose teams of agents to tackle complex jobs and trigger them to take action autonomously. Perception helps connect all the signals, sensors and actuators across your identity, client, cloud, apps and agents to intelligence to secure your end-to-end environments. And I am very excited to share that Perception is now generally available. In addition to the work we have been doing across our products, we are also working across the ecosystem to ensure everyone can innovate at speed and scale, safely. Today, we can see almost everything models touch. But we cannot see what happens inside the model. And what the model tells us about itself is not independent evidence. These nested black boxes are simply unacceptable. We need to be able to examine what AI sees and does, verify its actions independently and control what it is allowed to do. That is why today we are also announcing the Microsoft AI Transparency Initiative. There are three parts to this: First, we will expand our collaboration in NIST’s Agent Standards Initiative, drawing on its research to help lead the development of open, industry-wide standards for AI transparency, security and governance. Second, we are taking a full ecosystem approach. Together, we can enable AI systems that are accountable, independently verifiable and safe by design, regardless of the model or provider. Already, 40 organizations are working with us on defining and applying these standards. Third, we are working to incorporate the same standards in our products, including MAI models, Foundry and Copilot. Our ambition through our research, our product work and our ecosystem is to help establish an open industry standard that makes AI safer, more transparent and more accessible. Cobalt 200 VMs Underneath all of this is unbelievable silicon. We are building a heterogeneous platform working across the ecosystem to bring you all the latest innovation. We are also advancing our own hardware systems, co-designing silicon, servers and infrastructure to get more from every watt, chip and datacenter. We just announced Maia 300, which will deliver 40 percent more tokens per watt compared with leading GPU-based systems. Azure Boost and Azure Integrated HSM move critical infrastructure and security functions into purpose-built silicon. And today we are announcing general availability of our next-generation Cobalt 200 VMs, which are our highest-performing general-purpose VMs with leading price-performance. So, that is a quick walk through some of our news. When you look at all that is coming, it is clear that we are entering an era of ubiquitous intelligence. The key imperatives for us are to ensure human ambition, a firm’s control of its own intelligence and the diffusion of the benefits broadly. That is the promise of a frontier ecosystem. And that is what we are here to build together. For more information on today’s announcements, check out the Book of News . title: Four Continents, Four New AWS Heroes: Closing Out 2026
body: Four Continents, Four New AWS Heroes: Closing Out 2026 As AWS re:Invent is around the corner, we’re proud to recognize a new group of AWS Heroes . Every Hero finds their own way to give back, whether through sharing what they know, bringing people together, or building tools that help others succeed. What they have in common is a genuine commitment to supporting the builders around them learn, grow, and lead. Let us take a moment to meet them! Andres Moreno – El Paso, United States Serverless Hero Andres Moreno leads the Cloud del Norte AWS User Group and is a former AWS Community Builder. On his blog, And More Dev, and at conferences and community events, he explains serverless, cloud native architectures, generative AI, and agentic systems in ways that make new technology easier to try. Andres puts special energy into supporting builders across Latin America and helping them explore what’s possible on AWS. Geethika Guruge – Auckland, New Zealand Community Hero Geethika Guruge is a Principal Consultant at Mantel Group whose work spans serverless, DevOps, cloud infrastructure, and agentic AI. Geethika has shared real lessons from building agentic applications and leading large migration and modernization programs at AWS re:Invent, AWS Summits, and AWS Community Days. At home in Auckland, Geethika organizes local AWS meetups that encourage grassroots innovation and mentors the next generation of cloud architects and leaders. Jéssica Cristina Coelho – Belo Horizonte, Brazil Data Hero Jéssica Cristina Coelho is a Database Reliability Engineer and a former AWS Community Builder with more than 15 years of experience in databases, cloud, and data engineering. She leads the AWS User Group in Minas Gerais, hosts DataTalks Brasil, teaches MBA courses, and supports Women in Cloud, DevOpsDays, and AWS Community Day events. She speaks at events such as AWS Summit São Paulo and Web Summit Rio on database modernization and generative AI. At AWS re:Invent 2025, she was recognized as a LATAM Diversity & Inclusion Champion. Kazuho Cryer Shinozuka – Tokyo, Japan DevTools Hero Kazuho Cryer Shinozuka is an AWS CDK Top Contributor and Trusted CDK Community Reviewer. With 200 merged pull requests, he ranks 18th among more than 1,700 contributors. He has reviewed more than 120 pull requests, has been involved in about 2% of all CDK commits, and has published 10 construct libraries, along with tools such as cfn idle cost. Through talks at JAWS DAYS and CDK Conference Japan and through hands on contribution workshops, he helps more developers in Japan start contributing to open source. Learn More To connect with these Heroes or find one in your region, explore the AWS Heroes webpage , and join the conversation on AWS Builder Center . — Taylor

title: Ian Buck Kicks Off NVIDIA’s Week at SC26 as Science Enters the Age of Agents
body: Ian Buck Kicks Off NVIDIA’s Week at SC26 as Science Enters the Age of Agents At SC26, NVIDIA’s VP of Hyperscale and HPC laid out how researchers can combine simulation, AI and agents to accelerate scientific discovery. November 17, 2026 by Brian Caulfield 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! NVIDIA’s Ian Buck kicked off the company’s week at SC26 in Chicago on Monday with new tools for AI agents, software that can plan experiments, run code and check results on researchers’ own systems. In NVIDIA’s special address, Buck announced Nemotron for Science , the Rubin HPC GPU and an expanded Vera CPU platform for high-performance computing . He also detailed a new collaboration in quantum computing with IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory . “The frontier of computing and the new scientific stack is going to be simulation, as always, but combined with AI and the future of quantum,” said Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. Buck opened the talk by looking back to his first public talk on CUDA, at an SC06 tutorial in Tampa, Florida, 20 years ago. NVIDIA now offers more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries , he said. Open Models for Science Agents “[Agents] have been just a game changer in how we interface with our supercomputers, with our devices, our instruments and how we can do the research,” Buck said. Simulation remains the foundation of scientific computing, “which will always be on the top,” Buck said, with AI, quantum and now agents working alongside it. Nemotron for Science combines the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL open model with a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes for life sciences and chemistry, Buck explained. Researchers can run it locally on a DGX Spark, a workstation or their own supercomputer. At Argonne National Laboratory, Buck said, an agent built with the toolkit took a single prompt, planned and tested hypotheses, chose which simulations to run and identified two new binding sites. “You own your data. You own the model,” Buck said. Buck highlighted other agents already in use: GROMACS: An agent from KTH Royal Institute of Technology repairs broken GROMACS setups on its own. In one overnight run on a single DGX Spark, it fixed 81% of test cases. SETI Institute: At the Allen Telescope Array, an agent took a one-line prompt to plot a methanol line. Buck explained that it then retuned for Doppler shift on its own [NGC 869 vs. 896, check slide]. Nsight AI Porting Agent: NVIDIA’s new agent ported a routine from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to GPUs, Buck said, speeding it up more than 5x using about 150 million tokens. CPUs for the Agent Loop Agents lean on CPUs to run tool calls between model steps, Buck explained. “That’s exactly what agents need,” he said. “They need a CPU that can run, evaluate, run the tool, perform the operations, gather the results.” DKRZ, the German Climate Computing Center, has selected Vera CPUs for its HLRE-5 supercomputer, expected in early 2028. Buck said it joins Vera systems already announced at Texas Advanced Computing Center. A New GPU for Science Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the Vera Rubin platform, built for science, engineering, analytics and AI, Buck said. It supports precisions from FP64 to FP4, adds sparse-data acceleration and connects over seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink. With more than 50,000 CUDA cores, it has about three times as many as Hopper, Buck said. It is expected in 2028. Quantum Error Correction Buck said a simulation on Jülich’s JUPITER supercomputer showed that a technique called magic state cultivation can cut the operations needed for one logical step tenfold. The work is being added to CUDA-Q. NVIDIA, IBM and Fermilab announced plans today for a quantum computing co-design platform to support error-correction and applications research. NVIDIA and IBM are pairing NVIDIA DGX B200 systems with IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk. Buck also introduced a new breakthrough for quantum decoding. The goal, Buck explained, is to cut decoding latency from about 300 microseconds to 10. A new CUDA-Q decoding algorithm, TCBP-JOBS, cuts error-correction research computation from 12 weeks to 45 minutes, he said. Networking Buck also showed one of the first deployments of NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics switches, at Lambda . He said they are 15x more reliable on bit errors and link flaps. See notice regarding software product information. Mia Nagawiecki and Chance Coughenour are celebrating 100 years of Colonial Williamsburg by bringing its history to your screen. You can now explore thousands of newly digitized manuscripts, rare archival photos, and interactive galleries from home. These collections highlight the lives of ordinary people and the work behind preserving early American history. You can visit the Google Arts & Culture website to view these treasures, read new stories, and learn about 18th-century traditions. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Today, as Colonial Williamsburg marks its 100th anniversary, Google Arts & Culture is sharing new immersive stories and newly digitized cultural artifacts that honor a century of preservation, discovery, and public access. These additions expand on the digital hub we launched earlier this year with The Colonial Williamsburg Foundation to celebrate America’s 250th birthday and bring the rich history of early America online. Discover the latest stories and archives We’re introducing three new ways to explore Colonial Williamsburg’s legendary collections, taking you behind the scenes of how history is preserved, studied, and brought to life. Step inside an immersive online gallery : Learn about the Historic Area’s restoration, which began in 1926. This interactive gallery pairs rare archival photos with modern photography and period music across the first three reconstructed sites: the Governor’s Palace , the Raleigh Tavern , and the Capitol. Browse more than 3,000 new digital records : Through our ongoing collaboration, a specialized high-resolution tabletop scanner has helped digitize tightly bound volumes, delicate manuscripts, and centuries-old records. Today, we’re launching over 3,000 newly scanned images — including rare issues of the Virginia Gazette , fragile archival records, and special collections assets — making many of these treasures accessible to the public online for the very first time. Read new stories celebrating 100 years : New immersive stories capture the breadth of Colonial Williamsburg’s work and collections. Ranging from rare natural history surveys and early newspapers to reproductions and everyday items , these narratives explore the complex tapestry of American history through the experiences of ordinary people and the vital legacies of historically marginalized voices — and showcase the behind-the-scenes work keeping their histories alive. Explore newly digitized plates from naturalist Mark Catesby’s 18th-century masterwork, bringing 220 hand-engraved illustrations of North American wildlife and flora into brilliant, high resolution. Step inside the new online gallery to see the restoration of Colonial Williamsburg, spotlighting its first three reconstructed sites: the Governor's Palace, the Raleigh Tavern, and the Capitol. Dive into vivid watercolor and ink pages from folk artist Lewis Miller’s 19th-century sketchbook, offering a rare and powerful window into everyday Virginia life and the domestic slave trade. Discover historic American transportation through a rare folio of carriage drawings, showcasing the visual diversity of Colonial Williamsburg's library collections. Uncover the story of “Authentic Colors from Colonial Williamsburg” — a rare book featuring metal pages coated in historic automotive paints inspired by Colonial Williamsburg — and its unique conservation journey. Step into the kitchen with Max Miller’s “Tasting History” In partnership with Colonial Williamsburg and YouTube, culinary historian Max Miller, creator of “Tasting History,” visited the living history museum to film an exclusive episode , bringing 18th-century traditions to life. Praising the museum’s meticulous historical accuracy, Miller worked alongside Ivey Boyd, chef de cuisine at the King’s Arms Tavern, to prepare snow eggs ( oeufs à la neige ). This French dessert was popularized in early America by James Hemings, Thomas Jefferson's enslaved chef, and is served today at Colonial Williamsburg. This collaboration bridges traditional preservation with modern storytelling, inviting a new generation to discover the flavors and stories of early America. Look ahead to the next century of access By expanding access to Colonial Williamsburg’s collections, we’re safeguarding centuries-old treasures while sharing their history with the world. As Colonial Williamsburg enters its second century, we invite you to experience these new stories, archival records, and the living history of early America in a whole new way. title: Justice Department, VA, and VA OIG Announce Enforcement Actions Against 15 Defendants for Defrauding Veterans Benefits Programs
body: Press Release Justice Department, VA, and VA OIG Announce Enforcement Actions Against 15 Defendants for Defrauding Veterans Benefits Programs Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs 17 U.S. Attorney’s Offices joined the Fraud Division, Department of Veterans Affairs, and Department of Veterans Affairs Office of Inspector General in bringing charging actions against alleged 15 fraudsters The Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, along with the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), and VA Office of Inspector General today announced a nationwide series of enforcement actions targeting VA benefit fraud and related offenses amid National Veterans Awareness Week. Between Sept. 1, 2026, and today, the Fraud Division and 17 U.S. Attorneys’ Offices across the country participated in the Division’s first-ever coordinated national surge focusing on VA Benefits. The nationwide focus resulted in charges against 15 defendants whose alleged and proven crimes intended an estimated loss of revenue to the federal government of more than $3.4 million. The surge also included sentencings, pleas, and trial verdicts totaling more than $19 million in intended loss for the same time frame. In addition to the announced enforcement actions, the Fraud Division announced that U.S. Attorneys Ryan Raybould, Aaron Reitz, Justin Simmons, and Jay Combs joined with other law enforcement partners to create the Texas Federal Fraud Task Force. The task force will be comprised of all four U.S. Attorney’s Offices in Texas and will be supported by federal, state, and local law enforcement. The goal of the Task Force is straightforward: tirelessly combat fraud across the state of Texas. “For veterans, benefits are not simply government payments,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division. “They are earned benefits — earned through service, sacrifice, deployments, injuries, time away from loved ones, and a willingness to serve something larger than themselves. Today's results demonstrate the Department of Justice's commitment to protecting those who have served our nation, safeguarding taxpayer resources, and preserving the integrity of federal programs.” “Veterans and their families deserve protection from anyone seeking to exploit their service or steal the benefits they earned,” said Inspector General Cheryl Mason for the Department of Veterans Affairs. “The VA OIG works aggressively to identify fraud across the entire VA enterprise and hold offenders accountable. We strive every day to shield veterans from financial harm, safeguard VA resources, and preserve the public’s trust.” “When you defraud the VA, you defraud veterans who are owed benefits and you defraud the taxpayer for providing them,” said U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas. “My office is doing its part to protect the integrity of the VA, bring fraudsters to justice, and give veterans the confidence that I’ve got their backs.” “Fraudsters who exploit programs designed to serve veterans and servicemembers are stealing from the very people who answered our nation’s call to serve,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould for the Northern District of Texas. “Together with our law enforcement partners and fellow U.S. Attorneys across Texas, we are committed to protecting taxpayer-funded programs and holding accountable those who seek to profit at the expense of America’s veterans and military families.” “Here in the Eastern District of Texas, we are proud to be home to multiple VA facilities and an important U.S. Army installation,” said U.S. Attorney Jay R. Combs for the Eastern District of Texas. “Because we understand and value those who serve our nation, we take fraud targeting veterans and VA resources seriously,” said United States Attorney Jay R. Combs. “As a veteran myself, I know firsthand that benefits provided by the Department of Veterans Affairs are earned through service and sacrifice, and theft from those programs is an affront to the men and women who wore the uniform.  It will not be tolerated in the Eastern District of Texas.” “When somebody defrauds the VA, they are stealing from the honorable men and women who have served this nation and from the taxpayers who fund a collective commitment to support our veterans,” said U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas. “As federal prosecutors, justice is our North Star. With justice ever in mind, we will continue to pursue those who exploit the military community and steal from resources meant to support those who served to ensure all Americans can enjoy the blessings of freedom.” Image of the Cancer Infusion Therapy Center project, where the defendants allegedly defrauded the VA to secure a construction contract, leaving the project unfinished and ultimately resulting in the facility's demolition without replacement. Image of firearms seized during the execution of a search warrant in U.S. v. Zachary Somers Hiscock and Arif Hasan Sayed. During the search, investigators recovered unsecured loaded firearms and marijuana from a residence occupied by young children, leading to a referral to child protective services. Notable Cases **These cases are only a sample of the cases that have been included in the surge event** 1) U.S. v. Heidi Brady (6:26-CR-00215) (Indictment) | Western District of Texas According to the indictment, Heidi Brady, a Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) National Call Center employee in Killeen, Texas, abused her access to veterans' information to divert VA disability payments to a bank account she controlled. Brady allegedly used information obtained through her interactions with veterans and her knowledge of VA payment processing procedures to change direct deposit information shortly before monthly benefit payments were issued. This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Mark Frazier and Gregg Gloff for the Western District of Texas. District Fraud Counsel AOR: Assistant U.S. Attorney Justin Chung. 2) U.S. v. Yolanda Johnson Sayed (4:26-CR-699) (Information) | Southern District of Texas Yolanda Johnson Sayed, 61, of Houston, Texas, was charged with criminal information with conspiracy to commit wire fraud in connection with a scheme that allegedly defrauded the VA of approximately $182,000 through inflated delivery fees for prosthetic equipment. According to the charging document, Sayed, a prosthetics representative at the Houston VA Medical Center, conspired with the owner of a VA-approved vendor to steer purchase orders to the company and approve inflated delivery charges. Sayed allegedly used government-issued purchase cards to pay the fraudulent invoices and received a share of the proceeds through electronic transfers. Between November 2020 and August 2025, she allegedly conducted approximately 1,437 transactions with the vendor. The scheme involved mobility equipment, including wheelchairs and walkers. The government seeks forfeiture of at least $182,000 in fraud proceeds. This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Tina Ansari for the Southern District of Texas. District Fraud Counsel AOR: Kathryn Olson. 3) U.S. v. Michael Christopher Comiskey (1:26-cr-60284) (Indictment) | Southern District of Florida Michael Christopher Comiskey was charged with theft of government funds and aggravated identity theft in connection with a scheme involving VA benefits paid after the death of a veteran beneficiary. According to the indictment, Comiskey unlawfully converted federal benefit payments that continued after the veteran's death and used the deceased beneficiary's personal identifying information in furtherance of the scheme. Investigators allege that approximately $69,916 in VA benefits were improperly obtained. If convicted, Comiskey faces up to 10 years in prison on each theft of government funds count, as well as a mandatory consecutive two-year sentence for aggravated identity theft. This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nikole Hiciano for the Southern District of Florida. District Fraud Counsel AOR: Assistant U.S. Attorney Sally Molloy. 4) U.S. v. Darlene Toman (26-CR-475) (Indictment) | Northern District of Ohio According to the indictment, Darlene Toman exploited her position of trust by stealing from disabled veterans whose finances she was responsible for managing. The veteran victims suffered from serious physical and mental health conditions, including schizophrenia, traumatic brain injuries, epilepsy, heart failure, amputations, and bipolar disorder. Some required around-the-clock care and were unable to independently manage their finances. One victim, a decorated U.S. Marine Corps veteran who was severely wounded in combat in Iraq, received numerous military honors, including the Purple Heart and Combat Action Ribbon. Rather than safeguard funds intended to support these veterans, Toman allegedly used their identities and financial accounts to divert benefits for her personal use. The indictment alleges that she drafted fraudulent checks payable to herself and unlawfully converted veterans' benefit payments intended to cover essential living expenses and care. As alleged, Toman stole more than $940,000 from the victims. The victims included not only the veterans receiving VA benefits, but also the law firm where she was employed. This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Brenna Fasko for the Northern District of Ohio. District Fraud Counsel AOR: Brian McDonough. 5) U.S. v. Shawn Lightfoot (26-MJ-2055) (Complaint) | District of Columbia As alleged, Shawn Lightfoot engaged in a systematic scheme to defraud his neighbor, a 78-year-old disabled Veteran whose primary sources of income were Social Security benefits and VA disability payments. As part of the scheme, Lightfoot infiltrated the Victim’s financial accounts, opened credit card accounts in the victim's name, and used the Victim’s funds, which overwhelmingly consisted of VA compensation, to finance Lightfoot’s businesses. Lightfoot allegedly used the cards to conduct transactions in the veteran’s name, and directed funds and purchases to his own businesses, which included Das Food, a vegetarian catering company, and Art-drenaline, a café inside the Anacostia Art Center. The credit union also provided investigators with a recording of a May 25, 2025, phone call. During that call Lightfoot falsely claimed that he was the veteran, who at the time was incapacitated at a VA medical facility. When the credit union representative asked Lightfoot for verification and for photographic proof that he was the veteran, Lightfoot allegedly terminated the call.  As alleged, Lightfoot stole approximately $150,000. This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Kadian D. Carter for the District of Columbia. District Fraud Counsel AOR: Nicholas Reck. 6) U.S. v. Zachary Somers Hiscock and Arif Hasan Sayed (6:25-cr-204-CEM-DCI) (Jury Verdict) | Middle District of Florida Following trial, Zachary Somers Hiscock and Arif Hasan Sayed were convicted for their roles in a scheme to circumvent VA rules designed to protect veterans from predatory recruiting practices. Hiscock operated New Horizons of Phoenix in Arizona, while Sayed operated ABCO Technology in California. Evidence at trial showed that the defendants paid recruiters based on the amount of GI Bill tuition benefits generated by enrolled veterans, despite federal rules prohibiting commission-based recruitment of veterans. Veterans were promised valuable cybersecurity and information technology training and lucrative employment opportunities. Instead, many exhausted a year of GI Bill benefits for programs lasting only a few months and often received little meaningful certification or job placement assistance. The defendants also took steps to conceal the scheme by making false certifications to regulators, using coded terminology, and falsifying records. As a result of the fraud, revenue derived from VA education benefits increased dramatically at both schools. New Horizons of Phoenix's VA-related revenue grew from approximately $65,000 in 2018 to $2.28 million in 2021, while ABCO Technology's VA-related revenue increased from approximately $359,000 to $2.92 million during the same period. This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Matthew Del Mastro and Daniel Ley for the Middle District of Florida. District Fraud Counsel AOR: Assistant U.S. Attorney Jay Trezevant. 7) U.S. v. Matthew West and Kevin Kutina (8:23-cr-308-WFJ-AEP) (Jury Verdict) | Middle District of Florida In 2016, the VA solicited bids for the construction of the Cancer Infusion Therapy Center at Bay Pines VA Medical Center in Florida. The $8.9 million contract was reserved for Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned Small Businesses (SDVOSBs). Evidence at trial established that Matthew West, Kevin Kutina, and their co-conspirators secured the contract through false statements and material omissions regarding who would perform and manage the work. Although the contract was awarded to a qualifying SDVOSB, undisclosed agreements showed that non-qualifying entities would perform most of the work and receive the majority of the contract payments. After obtaining the contract, the conspirators continued to conceal the fraud through false statements and omissions submitted to the VA. The U.S. Treasury ultimately paid approximately $4.8 million under the contract, with millions of dollars flowing to entities that were not eligible for the SDVOSB set-aside program. The project was plagued by construction failures, resulting in the partially completed Cancer Infusion Therapy Center being demolished and never rebuilt. Co-defendants Robert and William Gonzalez pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Following trial, West and Kutina were convicted of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, and major fraud against the United States. This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tiffany Fields and Samantha Newman for the Middle District of Florida. District Fraud Counsel AOR: Assistant U.S. Attorney Jay Trezevant. 8 ) U.S. v. Barbara Ferrell (26-cr-80) (Sentencing) | Southern District of West Virginia According to court documents and statements made in court, from October 20, 2021, through March 11, 2024, Ferrell served as the VA appointed fiduciary for the family member. As part of her guilty plea, Ferrell admitted that from April 13, 2022, through Feb. 29, 2024, she knowingly and fraudulently took VA fiduciary benefits meant for the family member totaling approximately $114,660.82. Ferrell stole the benefit funds by periodically withdrawing the money once it had been electronically deposited for the family member in a joint checking account. Ferrell admitted that she spent the funds meant to benefit the family member for her own use and enjoyment. This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney and District Fraud Counsel Erik S. Goes for the Southern District of West Virginia. title: Texas Man Pleads Guilty to Sex Trafficking
body: Press Release Texas Man Pleads Guilty to Sex Trafficking Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Louisiana shane.jones@usdoj.gov NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA – U.S. Attorney David I. Courcelle announced that BRIAN KEITH HICKS (“HICKS”) , age 27, plead guilty to one count of Sex Trafficking by Force, Fraud, or Coercion, in violation of Title 18, United States Code, Sections 1591(a)(1), (a)(2), and (b)(1). According to court documents, BRIAN KEITH HICKS, a/k/a “Anthony Norton,” a/k/a “PMoneyy,” a/k/a “Pablo Money,” a/k/a “Kinfolks,” a/k/a “ Daddy” met an adult victim on social media in May 2025.  Shortly thereafter, HICKS taught her how to be a commercial sex worker. HICKS advertised the victim for sex online and transported her to various cities, including Dallas, Texas; Baton Rouge, Louisiana; New Orleans, Louisiana; Miami, Florida; Ft. Lauderdale, Florida; Tampa, Florida; and Jackson, Mississippi. Plea documents state that HICKS required the victim to earn approximately $1,000 a day from commercial sex transactions and provide him with all the proceeds.  If the victim did not make enough money for HICKS , did not want to engage in commercial sex work, or wanted to leave him, HICKS slapped or beat the victim. HICKS also kept the victim’s birth certificate as a means of control and required the victim to share her phone location with him so that he could monitor her movements.  On February 16, 2026, HICKS was arrested in New Orleans. HICKS continued to direct the victim to engage in commercial sex over recorded calls while he was in custody. During these jail calls, HICKS threatened to dislocate the victim’s jaw, punch her in the face, and kill her. HICKS faces a minimum of fifteen (15) years up to a maximum of life imprisonment, followed by a term of supervised release for a minimum of five (5) years up to a maximum of life, and a fine of up to $250,000.  Additionally, HICKS will be required to register as a sex offender.  In his plea agreement, HICKS agreed to pay restitution in the amount of $272,994.55 to the victim.  A $100.00 special assessment fee is also applicable. The Honorable Barry W. Ashe set sentencing for February 25, 2027. U.S. Attorney Courcelle praised the work of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Investigations, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, and the New Orleans Police Department in investigating this case.  Assistant United States Attorney and Human Trafficking and Child Exploitation Task Force Leader Maria M. Carboni of the Public Integrity Unit is in charge of the prosecution. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys' Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit Justice.gov/PSC . *   *   * Contact Shane M. title: Justice Department Surpasses $1B In Awards Under Reauthorized Radiation Exposure Compensation Act
body: Press Release Justice Department Surpasses $1B In Awards Under Reauthorized Radiation Exposure Compensation Act Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs The Justice Department announced today that it has awarded more than $1 billion in compassionate compensation to newly eligible claimants under the recently reauthorized Radiation Exposure Compensation Act (RECA). RECA was originally enacted in 1990 as a non-adversarial alternative to litigation for individuals who contracted certain illnesses following exposure to radiation as a result of the United States’ atmospheric nuclear testing program and uranium ore processing operations during the Cold War. The law sunset in 2024 and the Department ceased accepting new claims. In 2025, as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Congress reauthorized the law and expanded the scope of the RECA’s coverage. “We are proud that the Civil Division has delivered more than $1 billion in compensation to Americans under the reauthorized Radiation Exposure Compensation Act. Congress determined that these individuals deserve compensation, and the Civil Division is honored to help ensure they receive the benefits that Congress provided,” said Acting Assistant Attorney General Jonathan Guynn of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “This extraordinary law provides partial restitution to individuals and their families who were subject to increased risk of disease to serve the national security interests of the United States. I am especially proud of the extraordinary work of our team in administering this program efficiently and expeditiously, while remaining faithful to the law. This achievement reflects the dedication and professionalism of the Division’s attorneys and staff who made it possible, in addition to this law’s supporters in Congress who continue to make valuable contributions and provide support.” In its present form, RECA provides lump sum compensation awards to individuals who contracted specified diseases in four defined populations: “downwinders,” who are individuals who developed certain cancers after presumed exposure to radiation released during the atmospheric nuclear tests conducted within the United States between 1945 and 1962; “onsite participants” who participated in a test involving the atmospheric detonation of a nuclear device and later contracted a compensable disease; “uranium workers” who were employed in certain uranium extraction and processing occupations between 1942 and 1990; and individuals who developed a covered illness after living, working, or attending school in certain areas affected by Manhattan Project waste contamination. Compensation available under RECA ranges from $25,000 to $100,000 depending on the context of presumed exposure. RECA Compensation has been awarded to individuals residing in every state.  Since July 4, 2025, over 67,000 claims have been filed and over 14,000 claims have been approved.  Additional information is available on the Civil Division’s RECA website, www.justice.gov/civil/reca . Updated November 17, 2026 Component Civil Division Press Release Number: 26-1371

title: Illegal Alien With Multiple Deportations and a Drug Trafficking Conviction Charged for Illegal Reentry
body: Press Release Illegal Alien With Multiple Deportations and a Drug Trafficking Conviction Charged for Illegal Reentry Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Nevada LAS VEGAS – A Mexican national, with four prior deportations, made his initial court appearance Monday to face charges of illegally reentering the United States after previously being removed from the country. “Convicted drug traffickers who repeatedly defy our deportation orders and sneak back into our country are a direct threat to our communities, and we will throw the book at them,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada. “This district will not be a safe haven for foreign criminals who think they can ignore federal law and poison our neighborhoods. Under Operation Take Back America, if you are deported and come back illegally, we will hunt you down and prosecute you to the fullest extent of the law.” Ricardo Perez-Flores is charged with one count of deported alien found in the United States. A preliminary hearing is scheduled for November 30, 2026, before U.S. Magistrate Judge Elayna J. Youchah. According to allegations contained in the criminal complaint and statements made during court proceedings, Perez-Flores is a citizen and national of Mexico who was previously deported on or about January 30, 2013; March 19, 2019; July 24, 2019; and August 3, 2019, and reentered the United States illegally. On August 29, 2025, Henderson Police arrested Perez-Flores for trafficking a Schedule I or II controlled substance, flunitrazepam, or GHB, and possession of a Schedule I or II controlled substance, flunitrazepam, with intent to sell. Because record checks indicated that Perez-Flores is a citizen of Mexico who was illegally present in the United States after previously being removed, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) sent an immigration detainer. On November 5, 2026, the Nevada Department of Corrections remanded Perez-Flores to ICE custody in Las Vegas, Nevada. Perez-Flores has a felony conviction for trafficking a Schedule I or II controlled substance, flunitrazepam. If convicted, Perez-Flores faces the maximum statutory penalty of two years in prison, a one-year term of supervised release, a $250,000 fine, and a $100 special assessment. First Assistant United States Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada and Salt Lake City Field Office Director Jason Knight made the announcement. The ICE Salt Lake City, Las Vegas Sub-Office investigated this case; and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Nevada is prosecuting the case. Members of the public can report crimes and suspicious activity by dialing 866-DHS-2-ICE (866-347-2423) or completing the online tip form . This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime. A complaint is merely an accusation, and a defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. ### Updated November 17, 2026 Topics Operation Take Back America Immigration Component USAO - Nevada

title: Former Mobile County Sheriff’s Office Employee Pleads Guilty to Bank Fraud,  Money Laundering, and Tax Evasion
body: Press Release Former Mobile County Sheriff’s Office Employee Pleads Guilty to Bank Fraud,  Money Laundering, and Tax Evasion Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of Alabama MOBILE, AL – A Mobile man pleaded guilty today to bank fraud, money laundering, and tax evasion.  Daniel Holifield was previously scheduled for trial in December 2026 in the United States District Court.  After advising the Court last Wednesday that he intended to plead guilty, Holifield appeared before the Court today and entered his guilty plea. According to court documents, Holifield, a former Fleet Manager for the Mobile County Sheriff's Office, admitted using his position to steal funds through a scheme involving duplicate payments for vehicle repairs, equipment, and insurance claims.  Between 2021 and 2023, Holifield caused the same invoices to be submitted to both the Sheriff's Office and the Mobile County Commission.  After vendors were paid by the County Commission, he intercepted duplicate checks issued by the Sheriff's Office and deposited them into accounts he controlled. Holifield also admitted diverting insurance reimbursement checks and other payments intended for vendors or government entities for his personal use.  The fraud scheme generated approximately $277,814 in illicit proceeds.  As part of his guilty plea, Holifield admitted depositing the fraud proceeds into a Wells Fargo business account with little or no legitimate activity, transferring the funds to personal accounts, and then withdrawing or spending the money, including at casinos. He further admitted that he failed to report the fraud proceeds as income on his federal tax returns for 2021, 2022, and 2023, resulting in more than $105,000 in unpaid taxes. Sentencing is currently scheduled for February 22, 2027.  Holifield faces potential imprisonment, restitution, and other penalties to be determined by the court. “Daniel Holifield's guilty plea to federal charges of tax evasion, money laundering, and bank fraud confirms a serious betrayal of the public's trust and the trust placed in him by this Sheriff's Office,” said Mobile County Sheriff Paul Burch.  “When someone wears the badge, they are held to a higher standard, not a lower one.  No rank, title, or number of years of service puts anyone above the law.  The overwhelming majority of our deputies and employees serve this community with honesty, integrity, and dedication. They deserve better than to have their reputation tarnished by the criminal actions of one individual.  The badge is a symbol of public trust. Anyone who uses that trust for personal financial gain has no place in law enforcement.” “Mr. Holifield abused a position of trust to enrich himself at the expense of Mobile County taxpayers,” said United States Attorney Sean P. Costello. “Today's guilty plea demonstrates that those who steal public funds and attempt to conceal their crimes through the banking system and false tax filings will be held accountable.” This case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation, the Mobile County Sheriff’s Office, and other law enforcement partners. Assistant United States Attorney Kasee Heisterhagen is prosecuting the case on behalf of the United States. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. A copy of this press release may be found on the website of the United States Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Alabama at http://www.justice.gov/usao/als/ . body: Press Release Assistant Bank Manager Charged With Accepting Bribes Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Massachusetts Defendant allegedly took more than $50,000 to accept $28 million in bad checks for deposit BOSTON – An assistant bank manager has been arrested and charged with taking more than $50,000 in cash bribes in exchange for accepting $28 million in suspicious checks for deposit that ultimately did not clear. Luis Antonio Rego Bairos-Pirelli, 41, of Lowell, was charged with receipt of a bribe by a bank official. The defendant was arrested and was released on conditions following an initial appearance in federal court in Boston this afternoon. According to the charging documents, in or around 2023, a check casher began paying Bairos-Pirelli $1,000 in cash a week. In return, Bairos-Pirelli would allegedly, among other things, process checks for deposit (even if the bank’s anti-fraud software flagged the checks as suspicious) and make cash available for immediate withdrawal in violation of bank policy. Between Feb. 24, 2026 and April 20, 2026, more than $28 million of the check casher’s checks allegedly bounced, resulting in a loss of more than $1.5 million to the bank. The charge of receipt of a bribe by a bank official provides for a sentence of up to 30 years in prison, five years of supervised release and a fine of $1,000,000 or three times the amount of the bribes received. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case. United States Attorney Leah B. Foley; Brian Tucker, Special Agent in Charge of the Eastern Region of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Office of Inspector General; Thomas Demeo, Acting Special Agent in Charge of the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation, Boston Field Office; and Justin Page, Acting Inspector in Charge of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service’s Boston Division made the announcement. Valuable assistance was provided by the Lowell Police Department, the Massachusetts State Police and the Middlesex County Sheriff’s Office. Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam W. McCall of the Securities, Financial & Cyber Frauds Unit is prosecuting the case. The details contained in the charging document are allegations. The defendant is presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in the court of law. Updated November 17, 2026 Component USAO - Massachusetts

title: Plymouth Woman Sentenced for PPP Fraud and Money Laundering
body: Press Release Plymouth Woman Sentenced for PPP Fraud and Money Laundering Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Massachusetts BOSTON – A Plymouth woman was sentenced today in federal court in Boston for money laundering and submitting fraudulent Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan applications on behalf of herself and her father. Katherine Reynolds, 67, was sentenced by U.S. District Court Judge Myong J. Joun to three years’ probation. The defendant was also ordered to pay $41,666 in restitution. In February 2026 , Reynolds pleaded guilty to two counts of wire fraud and one count of money laundering. In August 2024 , Reynolds was indicted by a federal grand jury. Reynolds submitted two fraudulent loan applications seeking loans for herself and her father pursuant to the PPP. The loan applications falsely claimed that Reynolds and her then 86-year-old father earned over $100,000 per year providing massage services out of their home.  The loan applications also included fraudulent tax forms that were not filed with the IRS. After receiving the funds as a result of the fraudulent applications, Reynolds withdrew $20,000 in cash from the account into which the PPP loans were paid. United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and Jeff Grimming, Acting Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Investigations in New England made the announcement. The Massachusetts Office of the Inspector General provided valuable assistance in the investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorney Brian Sullivan of the Major Crimes Unit is prosecuting the case. On May 17, 2021, the Attorney General established the COVID-19 Fraud Enforcement Task Force to marshal the resources of the Department of Justice in partnership with agencies across government to enhance efforts to combat and prevent pandemic-related fraud. The Task Force bolsters efforts to investigate and prosecute the most culpable domestic and international criminal actors and assists agencies tasked with administering relief programs to prevent fraud by augmenting and incorporating existing coordination mechanisms, identifying resources and techniques to uncover fraudulent actors and their schemes, and sharing and harnessing information and insights gained from prior enforcement efforts. For more information on the department’s response to the pandemic, please visit https://www.justice.gov/coronavirus and https://www.justice.gov/coronavirus/combatingfraud . Anyone with information about allegations of attempted fraud involving COVID-19 can report it by calling the Department of Justice’s National Center for Disaster Fraud (NCDF) Hotline via the NCDF Web Complaint Form . Updated November 17, 2026 Topics Fraud COVID-Related Fraud Financial Fraud Component USAO - Massachusetts

title: Tajik National Convicted of Providing Material Support to ISIS and Firearms Offenses
body: Press Release Tajik National Convicted of Providing Material Support to ISIS and Firearms Offenses Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs The Defendant Sent Tens of Thousands of Dollars to ISIS Members Overseas, Used a Sham Marriage to Try to Obtain Status, and Illegally Possessed Firearms and Ammunition A federal jury in Brooklyn today convicted Mansuri Manuchekhri, also known as “Mansuri Manchekhri” and “Manysher,” on four counts of an indictment charging him with conspiring to provide material support to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS) and the Islamic State-Khorasan Province (ISIS-K), conspiring to possess and possessing firearms and ammunition while unlawfully in the United States, and making false statements to federal agents. On October 30, 2026, Manuchekhri pleaded guilty to a fifth count charging immigration fraud relating to a sham marriage between the defendant and a U.S. citizen. The verdict was returned following a two-week trial. When sentenced, Manuchekhri faces up to 55 years in prison. “Manuchekhri is a dangerous illegal alien who glorified ISIS’s violence, facilitated payments to ISIS-linked operatives, and unlawfully possessed firearms while living in the United States,” said Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General M. Scott Proctor. “His support for a terrorist organization responsible for murder and atrocities around the world, disregard for our nation’s laws, and obvious hatred of the United States made him a grave danger to the public. Today’s verdict demonstrates that those who aid terrorists will be held fully accountable.” “The defendant sent money to ISIS, a bloodthirsty terrorist organization, while training with assault rifles and proclaiming to his associates: ‘I am ready,’” said U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York. “But it is we who were ready, along with our law enforcement partners. The defendant’s conviction has neutralized a serious threat and shown the world that we will be unrelenting in dismantling terrorist funding networks.” “Mansuri Manuchekhri's alleged extremist plans were disrupted by the outstanding work of the New York Joint Terrorism Force,” said Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr. of the FBI New York Field Office. “He spent years living in New York while supporting ISIS and declaring his allegiance to the group. Today, he is off the streets. Anyone who seeks to support or commit terrorism should know that justice will find you.” As proven at trial, in June 2016, Manuchekhri traveled to the United States from Tajikistan on a non-immigrant tourist visa and unlawfully remained in the United States after his visa expired in December 2016. While in the United States, Manuchekhri collected jihadist propaganda videos that promoted violence and martyrdom and expressed his support for ISIS, praising past ISIS attacks in the United States such as the October 2017 West Side Highway truck attack that killed eight people and seriously injured many others. Manuchekhri’s ex-wife testified that he told her about the terrorist who carried out that deadly attack: “That guy is in heaven.” From approximately December 2021 through June 2023, while residing in Brooklyn, Manuchekhri facilitated approximately $70,000 in payments to ISIS-affiliated co-conspirators in Turkey and Syria, including to an individual who was later arrested by Turkish authorities for his alleged involvement in a January 2024 terrorist attack on a church in Istanbul for which ISIS-K publicly claimed responsibility. In March 2017, Manuchekhri paid an American citizen to enter into a sham marriage with him so that he could obtain legal status in the United States. However, he failed to provide certain supporting documentation that was requested by the government, and his petition was never granted. Within the same time frame as the money transfers, Manuchekhri possessed and used firearms and made frequent visits to shooting ranges even though he was prohibited from doing so as an alien unlawfully in the United States. In February 2022, he recorded himself firing an assault rifle at a shooting range in New Jersey and sent the video to one of the ISIS-affiliated individuals in Turkey with the message, “Thank God, I am ready, brother.” An invoice from the shooting range reflects that on Feb. 27, 2022, Manuchekhri and his friend rented a rifle port, an AK-47, and a Smith & Wesson M&P 15 tactical rifle, and purchased ammunition. Manuchekhri also possessed firearms elsewhere. On Aug. 24, 2024, Manuchekhri sent a different roommate a video recorded from inside a moving vehicle showing his outstretched arm firing a handgun out the window along a highway. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Andrew D. Reich and Lindsey R. Oken for the Eastern District of New York are prosecuting the case, with valuable assistance from Assistant U.S. Attorney Robert Pollack; Trial Attorney John Cella and Ryan White of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section; and Paralegal Specialist Wayne Colon. Updated November 17, 2026 Topic National Security Components Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) National Security Division (NSD) USAO - New York, Eastern Press Release Number: 26-1374

title: Mississippi Businessman Sentenced to 10 Years in Prison for $19M Medicare Fraud
body: Press Release Mississippi Businessman Sentenced to 10 Years in Prison for $19M Medicare Fraud Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs A Mississippi businessman was sentenced yesterday to 10 years in prison for paying illegal kickbacks for fraudulent doctors’ orders and then using those orders to fraudulently bill Medicare over $19 million through seven different durable medical equipment (DME) supply companies. According to court documents, Willie De Gibbs, 53, of Toomsuba, Mississippi, and Cutler Bay, Florida, was the sole owner of three DME supply companies and the beneficial owner of and controlled, sometimes through straw owners, four other DME supply companies. Gibbs signed Medicare enrollment applications on behalf of some of these DME supply companies, certifying to Medicare that he would comply with all Medicare rules and regulations, including prohibitions on fraud, waste, and abuse, and that he would not violate the Federal Anti-Kickback Statute. Gibbs broke these promises by paying bribes and kickbacks to multiple companies in exchange for signed doctors’ orders for orthotic braces. Gibbs disguised the true nature of these illegal kickbacks through sham contracts for “marketing,” “advertising,” “telemedicine,” and “lead acquisition.” Gibbs then used these orders to bill Medicare for orthotic braces. The braces that Gibbs billed to Medicare through the seven DME supply companies were medically unnecessary. The doctors who ordered the braces did not have a pre-existing doctor-patient relationship with the Medicare patients, were not treating the patients, did not conduct a physical examination of the patients, and did not conduct a proper telemedicine visit. Gibbs also billed for braces that were never ordered by a physician at all. Indeed, one of the DME supply companies created doctors’ orders out of whole cloth by falsely appropriating the credentials of practitioners to justify the brace orders, unbeknownst to the practitioners. Gibbs received multiple complaints from Medicare patients, their family members, and others that the orthotic braces they received from Gibbs’ DME supply companies were never requested and were not needed. In many cases, Medicare patients received multiple braces. For example, one beneficiary received a back brace, two knee braces, and two suspension sleeves, for which Medicare paid $2,520 based on the fraudulent claims. In total, Gibbs caused approximately $19,455,116 in false and fraudulent claims to Medicare. Medicare paid approximately $9,460,142 based on these claims. Gibbs pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit health care fraud in November 2025. In addition to the prison term, Gibbs was ordered to pay $9,460,142.27 in restitution. Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division; Special Agent in Charge Robert A. Eikhoff of the FBI Jackson Field Office; and Acting Deputy Inspector General for Investigations Scott J. Lampert of the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG) made the announcement. The FBI Jackson Field Office and HHS-OIG investigated the case. Deputy Chief Sara E. Porter of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Kimberly T. Purdie for the Southern District of Mississippi prosecuted the case. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/fraud/health-care-fraud-section . Updated November 17, 2026 Topic Fraud Component National Fraud Enforcement Division Press Release Number: 26-1368

title: PACE Organization InnovAge Agrees to Pay $36M to Resolve False Claims Act Allegations of Failing to Provide Comprehensive Medical Services and Timely Specialist Referrals to Seniors
body: Press Release PACE Organization InnovAge Agrees to Pay $36M to Resolve False Claims Act Allegations of Failing to Provide Comprehensive Medical Services and Timely Specialist Referrals to Seniors Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs InnovAge Holding Corporation (InnovAge), headquartered in Denver, Colorado, has agreed to pay a total of $36 million to resolve allegations that it violated the federal False Claims Act and state laws by failing to provide required comprehensive medical services and timely referrals to medical specialists as expeditiously as its patients’ health conditions required. “Failing to provide comprehensive medical services and timely specialist referrals threatens the health of our most vulnerable seniors,” said Acting Assistant Attorney General Jonathan D. Guynn of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “This historic, first-of-its-kind settlement demonstrates the Civil Division’s commitment to combating healthcare fraud by PACE organizations.” “Elderly patients suffer when PACE providers like InnovAge do not fulfill their obligations to schedule patient visits with medical specialists in a timely manner,” said U.S. Attorney Peter McNeilly for the District of Colorado. “The U.S. Attorney’s Office in Colorado is committed to holding PACE providers accountable to ensure they provide comprehensive and timely care.” “PACE organizations that receive Medicare and Medicaid funding must meet their obligations to provide timely and comprehensive care to the vulnerable seniors they serve as delays can jeopardize the health of patients,” said Acting Deputy Inspector General for Investigations Miranda L. Bennett of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG). “This settlement demonstrates that organizations that fail to comply with those requirements will be held accountable. HHS-OIG remains committed to working with our law enforcement partners and leveraging the False Claims Act to help ensure providers comply with program requirements and deliver the care their patients need.” InnovAge provides services to seniors under a dual Medicare-Medicaid program called the Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE). InnovAge has PACE centers in several states, including California, Colorado, New Mexico, and the Commonwealth of Virginia. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) pays PACE organizations a fixed monthly amount for each Medicare beneficiary enrolled in their programs. In return, PACE organizations must provide comprehensive health care services to their participants, and all services must be provided as expeditiously as the participant’s health condition requires. This settlement resolves allegations that, from May 2016 to October 2022, InnovAge failed to provide comprehensive health care services as expeditiously as required by its patients. Specifically, InnovAge allegedly failed to maintain sufficient specialist provider networks and, in thousands of instances, InnovAge failed to timely schedule appointments or consultations for specialist medical care, such as for oncology, cardiology, surgery, and neurology, for its patients. The United States and various states further alleged that InnovAge’s internal reports of providers’ medical orders regularly showed numerous and recurrent delinquent specialist referrals. Several senior InnovAge physicians also complained to InnovAge about the company’s scheduling practices and delays for specialist referrals. These complaints included that InnovAge’s scheduling practices and delays had negative health care consequences for participants, placed legal risk on InnovAge’s healthcare providers, and put InnovAge out of compliance with CMS requirements. In addition, InnovAge’s internal audits found significant delays in specialist care, including numerous delayed orders, of which many were over a year outstanding. As a result of this settlement, InnovAge will pay approximately $25.7 million to the United States and a combined $10.3 million to the States of Colorado, California, and New Mexico, and the Commonwealth of Virginia. The civil settlement includes the resolution of federal and states’ claims brought under the qui tam or whistleblower provisions of the False Claims Act and analogous state statutes by two former employees, Monita Poudyal and Karen Lapcewich. Under those provisions, a private party can file an action on behalf of the United States and receive a portion of any recovery. The qui tam cases are captioned United States ex rel. Poudyal v. InnovAge Holding Corp., et al. , No. 1:21-cv-02464 (D. Colo.) and United States ex rel. Lapcewich v. Total Community Options Inc., et al. , No. 1:22-cv-01686 (D. Colo.). The relator share of the federal settlement will be $4.5 million. This year the Administration launched the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud and the National Fraud Enforcement Division to enhance the Administration’s war on fraud, waste, and abuse in federal programs. When unscrupulous actors exploit these programs for their own financial gain, they defraud the government, harm the people these programs are designed to aid and protect, and undermine American businesses that play by the rules. The Civil Division’s FCA enforcement plays a critical role in combatting such fraudulent schemes, recovering billions of dollars for the American taxpayers, and holding wrongdoers accountable. FCA matters will continue to be on the forefront of the battle against fraud, and the Civil Division’s FCA work will support and advance the mission of the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud and the National Fraud Enforcement Division. The resolution obtained in this matter was the result of a coordinated effort between the Justice Department’s Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section, and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Colorado, with assistance from the Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General. The investigation and resolution of this matter illustrates the government’s emphasis on combating healthcare fraud. One of the most powerful tools in this effort is the False Claims Act. Tips and complaints from all sources about potential fraud, waste, abuse, and mismanagement, can be reported to the Department of Health and Human Services at 800-HHS-TIPS (800-447-8477). Trial Attorneys Yifan Wang and David G. Miller of the Civil Division and Assistant U.S. Attorney Lila Bateman for the District of Colorado handled the matter. The claims resolved by the settlement are allegations only and there has been no determination of liability. Updated November 17, 2026 Topic False Claims Act Component Civil Division Press Release Number: 26-1366

Algerian man pleads guilty to his role in black market fraud conspiracy that targeted thousands of victims
body: Press Release Algerian man pleads guilty to his role in black market fraud conspiracy that targeted thousands of victims Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of New York BUFFALO, N.Y.-U.S. Attorney Michael DiGiacomo announced today that Abdellah Belmili, a/k/a Dila Belmili, a/k/a SPOX, 27, a citizen of Algeria, pleaded guilty before U.S. District Judge John L. Sinatra, Jr. to conspiracy to commit bank fraud, which carries a maximum penalty of 30 years in prison. According to the plea agreement, between March 2020 and January 2023, Belmili created and sold “phishing kits.” “Phishing” is the practice of sending fraudulent emails or text messages claiming to be from legitimate companies in order to induce a person to reveal personal information, such as their password or credit card number. A “phishing kit” is a package of software—such as source code, images, and computer scripts—that allows a cybercriminal to launch a phishing attack. The kit also allows the cybercriminal to generate a login page that looks identical to the legitimate company’s login page but sends the stolen credentials directly to the cybercriminal. Belmili sold his kits, as well as other hacking tools, through online marketplaces he operated and through his Telegram channel. In December 2020, an employee of the FBI in the Western District of New York, acting in an undercover capacity, created an account on Belmili’s online marketplace and made multiple purchases, including a phishing kit designed to replicate a JP Morgan Chase website. A phishing victim who was directed to the fraudulent JP Morgan Chase website would believe that they could enter their personal identifying information (PII), including their username, password, credit card number, security code, and mother’s maiden name. In reality, all such PII would be transmitted to the person who purchased the phishing kit from Belmili. He also created and sold similar phishing kits designed to replicate the websites of American Express, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo, which allowed Belmili’s customers to unlawfully access and obtain Funds, credits, assets, securities, and other property owned by each of these financial institutions. The phishing kits Belmili created and sold were used more than 1,000 times with Belmili receiving approximately $75,793.07 from the sale of the kits. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Charles M. Kruly. The plea is the culmination of an investigation by the FBI, under the direction of Special Agent-in-Charge Allen D. Davis, II. Sentencing will be scheduled at a later date before Judge Sinatra. # # # # Contact Barbara Burns 716-843-5817 Updated November 17, 2026 Topic Financial Fraud Component USAO - New York, Western
