title: Salinas Man Sentenced to Over 11 Years in Prison for Attempted Sexual Exploitation of a 12-Year-Old and Distributing Child Pornography
body: Press Release Salinas Man Sentenced to Over 11 Years in Prison for Attempted Sexual Exploitation of a 12-Year-Old and Distributing Child Pornography Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Donald Ramirez, 40, of Salinas, California, was sentenced to 138 months in prison and 15 years of supervised release for attempted enticement and coercion of a minor and for distribution of child pornography. He was also ordered to pay $72,000 in restitution. According to court documents, Ramirez used Snapchat to send a 12-year-old girl a photo of his genitals and repeatedly demanded that the child create and send him photos of herself engaged in sexually explicit conduct he directed. Ramirez also used other social media platforms, including Telegram and Wickr, to distribute child sexual abuse material including images of another female minor whom he had communicated with on Snapchat. Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division, U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian for the Northern District of California, and Special Agent in Charge SAC Jeff Brannigan of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) San Francisco made the announcement. HSI investigated the case. The Salinas Police Department, the Monterey County Probation Department, and the Monterey County District Attorney's Office assisted during the investigation. Trial Attorney McKenzie Hightower of the Justice Department’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS) and Assistant U.S. Attorney Neal Hong for the Northern District of California are prosecuting the case. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.justice.gov/psc . title: Iranian Intelligence Agent Sentenced to 330 Months in Prison for Foiled Plot to Assassinate U.S. Government Officials
body: Press Release Iranian Intelligence Agent Sentenced to 330 Months in Prison for Foiled Plot to Assassinate U.S. Government Officials Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of New York Defendant Attempted to Hire Hitmen to Murder President Donald J. Trump and  Other U.S. Government Officials on Behalf of Iran BROOKLYN, NY – Earlier today, in federal court in Brooklyn, Asif Merchant was sentenced by United States District Judge Eric R. Komitee to 330 months in prison for attempting to commit an act of terrorism transcending national boundaries and murder for hire.  Merchant, a Pakistani national, is a trained operative of the Iranian government’s global terrorist force, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).  Merchant was convicted by a federal jury in March 2026 of traveling to the United States to arrange for political assassinations on American soil. Todd Blanche, United States Attorney General; Joseph Nocella, Jr., United States Attorney for the Eastern District of New York; M. Scott Proctor, Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security; and James C. Barnacle, Assistant Director in Charge, Federal Bureau of Investigation, New York Field Office, announced the sentence. “An Iranian agent who came to the United States to coordinate an assassination attempt against President Trump has been justly sentenced for his criminal conduct,” stated Attorney General Blanche.  “The Department of Justice will not tolerate foreign terrorist plots against our leaders and will not stop until those responsible are held accountable.” “Today’s sentence ensures that Asif Merchant never again has the opportunity to plan an evil attack on America,” stated United States Attorney Nocella.  “Iran, its proxies, and its terrorist assets near and far should recognize this case as an example of U.S. law enforcement’s strength. If you plan an attack on our democracy, on our elected officials, on our people, we will stop you and prosecute you to the fullest extent of the law.” “The IRGC sent Merchant to avenge the strike on their terrorist commander, Qasem Soleimani,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security Proctor.  “Thanks to exceptional investigative and prosecutorial work by our federal law enforcement professionals, the plot failed.  The stiff sentence Merchant has now received should stand as a stark warning — if you come to America on behalf of a foreign power to commit terrorist acts, we will find you and lock you away.” Mr. Nocella expressed his appreciation to the FBI Field Offices in New York, Dallas, Houston, Tampa, Chicago, and Boston for their partnership on this case.  Mr. Nocella also expressed his appreciation to the U.S. Customs and Border Protection for their assistance. “The sentencing of Asif Merchant is a victory of the FBI’s mission to secure the homeland.  Merchant's plot against a prominent critic of the Iranian regime posed a serious threat to public safety and our national security.  Today's sentence demonstrates that anyone who seeks to use violence or intimidation to silence dissent will face justice.  The FBI Joint Terrorism Task force will continue to work tirelessly to root out the evils of terrorism,” stated FBI Assistant Director in Charge Barnacle. By his own admission, Merchant voluntarily joined the IRGC and became a trained intelligence asset.  He then traveled to the United States and, on behalf of the IRGC, located and paid hitmen to kill United States government officials.  Merchant believed that the ultimate target of his murder plot would be Donald J. Trump, but stated that other targets could have been then-President Joe Biden and former United Nations Ambassador Nikki Haley, all of whom were American presidential candidates at the time.  Merchant admitted that the murder plot was motivated by Iran’s desire to avenge the death of former IRGC commander Qasem Soleimani, who was killed in a U.S. drone strike in January 2020. As Merchant admitted in his trial testimony, he was recruited by the IRGC in approximately 2022.  At that time, Merchant began traveling to Iran on religious pilgrimages and, through a relative, was introduced to his IRGC handler, Yousef Merhardad.  Beginning in approximately 2023, Merchant met with his IRGC handler approximately 15 times over the course of a year and a half in Tehran, the capital of Iran. During those meetings, the IRGC handler trained Merchant on counterintelligence measures and tasked Merchant to travel to the United States to orchestrate a plot to assassinate United States government officials.  Merchant was instructed that the hitmen he hired should be criminals or Mafia members and that they should carry out the assassination at a political rally in the United States.  Merchant testified at trial that he believed the ultimate target of his plot was President Trump. In approximately April 2024, immediately after spending a week in Iran, Merchant flew to the United States to carry out his plot.  Once in the United States Merchant contacted an acquaintance to assist him with his assassination scheme.  Instead, the acquaintance reported Merchant to the FBI and served as an informant. In a video recording introduced at trial, Merchant methodically described a portion of his plot to the informant and mapped out the murder of a politician at a political rally.  Merchant then reached out to purported hitmen who were actually undercover FBI agents.  Merchant met three times with the purported hitmen and explained to them that he was working with people overseas and wanted to hire them to kill a politician.  Merchant then paid the purported hitmen $5,000 as an initial payment for the murder plot, which Merchant obtained with the assistance of overseas relatives.  After hiring the hitmen, Merchant was arrested in Richmond, Texas, on July 12, 2026, as he was about to go to the airport to leave the United States. Evidence obtained from Merchant’s laptop, cellphones, and social media accounts showed his focus on the 2024 presidential election and President Trump.  Materials introduced at trial included Merchant’s internet searches related to campaign rallies and a search using Google Maps for the location of a Trump rally in New Jersey.  Merchant’s social media accounts included posts praising Soleimani and targeting President Trump and the United States. The case is being handled by the Office’s National Security & Cybercrime Section.  Assistant United States Attorneys Sara K. Winik, Nina C. Gupta, and Gilbert M. Rein are in charge of the prosecution, with assistance from Paralegal Specialist Magdalena St. Surin and Deputy Chief Paul Casey of the Counterterrorism Section of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division. The Defendant : ASIF MERCHANT (also known as “Asif Raza Merchant”) Age: 48 Karachi, Pakistan; Tehran, Iran E.D.N.Y. title: D.C. Restauranteur Charged in Elder Financial Exploitation Scheme Against His Neighbor, a 78-Year-Old Disabled Veteran
body: Press Release D.C. Restauranteur Charged in Elder Financial Exploitation Scheme Against His Neighbor, a 78-Year-Old Disabled Veteran Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Columbia lightfoot_26-mj-205_affidavit_in_support_002_redacted.pdf WASHINGTON – Shawn Dmitrius Lightfoot, 62, of the District, was charged by complaint on November 10, 2026, in U.S. District Court in connection with an alleged systematic scheme that stole approximately $150,000 from his next-door neighbor, a 78-year-old disabled veteran, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro. Lightfoot was arrested today by U.S. Marshals and is scheduled to make his first appearance today. The complaint charges Lightfoot with one count of bank fraud, one count of aggravated identity theft, and one count of financial exploitation of an elderly person. According to the complaint, Lightfoot lived next door to the highly decorated Vietnam War combat veteran whose income consisted primarily of Social Security Payments and U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs disability payments. Through deception, Lightfoot gained access to the veteran’s finances, mail, disability payments, and personal identifying information. With that access, Lightfoot opened several credit cards using the veteran’s name, date of birth, and Social Security number, along with Lightfoot’s own email address and phone number. Lightfoot allegedly used the credit cards and the veteran’s pre-existing accounts to conduct transactions in the veteran’s name and directed funds and purchases to his own food service businesses. This investigation is being conducted by U.S. Postal Inspection Service and the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs Office of the Inspector General. It is being prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. An indictment, information, or complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. 26mj205 Updated November 17, 2026 Topics Elder Justice Fraud Financial Fraud Component USAO - District of Columbia

title: USAO Team Member Honored with National Award
Parker Man Sentenced For COVID-19 Related Fraud
body: Press Release Parker Man Sentenced For COVID-19 Related Fraud Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Colorado USACO.PublicAffairs@usdoj.gov DENVER – The United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Colorado announces that Tarek Mohamad Kassem, 66, Parker, Colorado, was sentenced to 18 months in federal prison, three years of supervised release, restitution totaling $2,041,649.51, and a forfeiture money judgement of $1,776,792.00 after pleading guilty to one count of wire fraud and one count of money laundering. According to the plea agreement and facts established at sentencing, from about March 2020 through February 2022, the defendant prepared and submitted fraudulent Economic Injury Disaster Loans (EIDL) and Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) applications to the Small Business Administration on behalf of business entities that he purportedly operated.  In these applications, Kassem made materially false statements regarding the entities’ number of employees, gross revenues, cost of goods sold, and monthly payrolls. After receiving more than $1.7 million in fraudulent loans, Kassem used the funds primarily for his own personal benefit, including purchasing vehicles and a house. “This type of fraud is direct theft from the American taxpayer, and the Department of Justice will not stand for it,” said United States Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “I am glad that our office and our federal partners continue to aggressively prosecute those who stole from the government during a time of crisis.” “Federal support to businesses during the pandemic was meant to keep workers and the economy afloat – not to enrich fraudsters. But like so many others, this defendant saw an opportunity to defraud the government and American taxpayers,” said FBI Denver Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski.  “Kassem should have known better, and now he can think about his mistake from behind prison bars.” “While the pandemic has ended, our pursuit of those who exploited COVID-19 relief programs at the expense of American families and small businesses has not,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Scott Brown, IRS-CI Phoenix Field Office. “We remain steadfast in our commitment to working with the U.S. Attorney’s Office to identify and investigate those who abused these programs for personal gain and ensure they are held accountable.” "This 18-month sentence, combined with nearly $3.8 million in restitution and forfeiture, sends a clear message: those who exploit pandemic relief programs for personal enrichment will face serious consequences,” said Department of Labor Office of Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito. “Kassem's fraudulent scheme represents an egregious betrayal of the emergency assistance meant to help struggling Americans. We remain committed to combating fraud wherever it occurs and are grateful to our federal partners for their continued collaboration.” “Unemployment insurance fraud is a serious crime that steals taxpayer dollars and undermines programs designed to support individuals and families in need,” said Joseph V. Cuffari, Ph.D., Department of Homeland Security Inspector General. “Those who exploit these programs for personal gain must be held accountable. We are grateful to our federal, state, and local law enforcement partners for their continued collaboration and commitment to investigating fraud, protecting public resources, and ensuring the integrity of these critical programs.” United States District Judge Nina Y. Wang presided over the sentencing. The FBI Denver Field Office, IRS-Criminal Investigation, the Department of Labor Office of the Inspector General, and the Department of Homeland Security Office of the Inspector General handled the investigation.  Assistant United States Attorney Nicole Cassidy handled the prosecution. The core mission of the National Fraud Enforcement Division is to zealously investigate and prosecute those who steal or fraudulently misuse taxpayer dollars. The National Fraud Enforcement Division will fulfill that mission by coordinating with agencies responsible for administering benefit programs; partnering with federal, tribal, state, territorial, and local law enforcement on fraud-fighting efforts; developing systems and processes that ensure efficient identification of fraud against taxpayer dollars; and equipping prosecutors and law enforcement with state-of-the-art tools and resources needed to bring criminal actors to justice. The attorneys in the National Fraud Enforcement Division will work every day to protect the financial integrity of our government and the tax system that supports it. Department of Justice efforts support President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. Anyone with information about allegations of attempted fraud involving COVID-19 can report it by calling the Department of Justice’s National Center for Disaster Fraud (NCDF) Hotline at 866-720-5721 or via the NCDF Web Complaint Form at: https://www.justice.gov/disaster-fraud/ncdf-disaster-complaint-form Case Number: 1:24-cr-00088-NYW Contact USACO.PublicAffairs@usdoj.gov Updated November 17, 2026 Component USAO - Colorado

title: Iranian Intelligence Agent Sentenced to Over 27 Years in Prison for Foiled Plot to Assassinate U.S. Government Officials
body: Press Release Iranian Intelligence Agent Sentenced to Over 27 Years in Prison for Foiled Plot to Assassinate U.S. Government Officials Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Defendant Attempted to Hire Hitmen to Murder President Donald J. Trump and  Other U.S. Government Officials on Behalf of Iran Earlier today, in federal court in Brooklyn, Asif Merchant, 48, of Pakistan, was sentenced by U.S. District Judge Eric R. Komitee to 330 months in prison for attempting to commit an act of terrorism transcending national boundaries and murder for hire. Merchant is a trained operative of the Iranian government’s global terrorist force, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Merchant was convicted by a federal jury in March 2026 of traveling to the United States to arrange for political assassinations on American soil. “An Iranian agent who came to the United States to coordinate an assassination attempt against President Trump has been justly sentenced for his criminal conduct,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The Department of Justice will not tolerate foreign terrorist plots against our leaders and will not stop until those responsible are held accountable.” “The IRGC sent Merchant to avenge the strike on their terrorist commander, Qasem Soleimani,” said Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Thanks to exceptional investigative and prosecutorial work by our federal law enforcement professionals, the plot failed.  The stiff sentence Merchant has now received should stand as a stark warning — if you come to America on behalf of a foreign power to commit terrorist acts, we will find you and lock you away.” “Today’s sentence ensures that Asif Merchant never again has the opportunity to plan an evil attack on America,” said U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York. “Iran, its proxies, and its terrorist assets near and far should recognize this case as an example of U.S. law enforcement’s strength. If you plan an attack on our democracy, on our elected officials, on our people, we will stop you and prosecute you to the fullest extent of the law.” “The sentencing of Asif Merchant is a victory of the FBI’s mission to secure the homeland,” said Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr. of the FBI New York Field Office. “Merchant's plot against a prominent critic of the Iranian regime posed a serious threat to public safety and our national security.  Today's sentence demonstrates that anyone who seeks to use violence or intimidation to silence dissent will face justice.  The FBI Joint Terrorism Task force will continue to work tirelessly to root out the evils of terrorism.” By his own admission, Merchant voluntarily joined the IRGC and became a trained intelligence asset. He then traveled to the United States and, on behalf of the IRGC, located and paid hitmen to kill U.S. government officials. Merchant believed that the ultimate target of his murder plot would be Donald J. Trump but stated that other targets could have been then-President Joe Biden and former United Nations Ambassador Nikki Haley, all of whom were American presidential candidates at the time. Merchant admitted that the murder plot was motivated by Iran’s desire to avenge the death of former IRGC commander Qasem Soleimani, who was killed in a U.S. drone strike in January 2020. As Merchant admitted in his trial testimony, he was recruited by the IRGC in approximately 2022. At that time, Merchant began traveling to Iran on religious pilgrimages and, through a relative, was introduced to his IRGC handler, Yousef Merhardad. Beginning in approximately 2023, Merchant met with his IRGC handler approximately 15 times over the course of a year and a half in Tehran, the capital of Iran. During those meetings, the IRGC handler trained Merchant on counterintelligence measures and tasked Merchant to travel to the United States to orchestrate a plot to assassinate U.S. government officials. Merchant was instructed that the hitmen he hired should be criminals or Mafia members and that they should carry out the assassination at a political rally in the United States. Merchant testified at trial that he believed the ultimate target of his plot was President Trump. In approximately April 2024, immediately after spending a week in Iran, Merchant flew to the United States to carry out his plot. Once in the United States, Merchant contacted an acquaintance to assist him with his assassination scheme. Instead, the acquaintance reported Merchant to the FBI and served as an informant. In a video recording introduced at trial, Merchant methodically described a portion of his plot to the informant and mapped out the murder of a politician at a political rally. Merchant then reached out to purported hitmen who were actually undercover FBI agents. Merchant met three times with the purported hitmen and explained to them that he was working with people overseas and wanted to hire them to kill a politician. Merchant then paid the purported hitmen $5,000 as an initial payment for the murder plot, which Merchant obtained with the assistance of overseas relatives. After hiring the hitmen, Merchant was arrested in Richmond, Texas, on July 12, 2026, as he was about to go to the airport to leave the United States. Evidence obtained from Merchant’s laptop, cellphones, and social media accounts showed his focus on the 2024 presidential election and President Trump. Materials introduced at trial included Merchant’s internet searches related to campaign rallies and a search using Google Maps for the location of a Trump rally in New Jersey. Merchant’s social media accounts included posts praising Soleimani and targeting President Trump and the United States. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Sara K. Winik Nina C. Gupta and Gilbert M. Rein for the Eastern District of New York are in charge of the prosecution with assistance from Paralegal Specialist Magdalena St. Surin and Deputy Chief Paul Casey of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section. title: Irish National Indicted For Destroying $60 Million U.S. Military C-130H Aircraft At Shannon Airport, Ireland
body: Press Release Irish National Indicted For Destroying $60 Million U.S. Military C-130H Aircraft At Shannon Airport, Ireland Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of New York United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald, and Assistant Director in Charge of the New York Field Office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (“FBI”), James C. Barnacle, Jr., announced charges against DAITHI O’CORRAIN, a/k/a “David Curran,” an Irish national, for breaking into and destroying a U.S. military C-130H aircraft (the “Aircraft”) parked at Shannon Airport in County Clare, Ireland. “These charges send a clear and powerful message that attacks on U.S. military assets—and thus our national security—will not be tolerated,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “As alleged in the indictment, the defendant destroyed a valuable U.S. military aircraft abroad and, in the process, posed a significant threat to others, including U.S. service members, nearby. This indictment holds the defendant accountable for his serious crime and serves as a warning to others, wherever they may be, considering similar criminal activity.” “As alleged, Daithi O’Corrain carried out a deliberate, planned attack against a U.S. military aircraft, causing tens of millions of dollars in damage and jeopardizing critical military operations,” said FBI Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle, Jr. “This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism. The defendant allegedly spent months researching the aircraft, acquiring tools and materials, and preparing to maximize the destruction he could inflict. The FBI and our law enforcement partners will continue to pursue anyone who targets U.S. military assets, regardless of where those attacks occur.” According to the allegations contained in the Indictment: On or about the morning of April 11, 2026, O’CORRAIN breached the security perimeter of Shannon Airport, which serves as a major transatlantic hub for U.S. military troops and equipment. O’CORRAIN then traversed the airport to the vicinity of the Aircraft, pictured below—a U.S. Air National Guard C-130 Hercules (“C-130H”) aircraft parked on the taxiway, en route to another country on U.S. military assignment. After reaching the Aircraft, O’CORRAIN gained entry by breaking the locking mechanism on the Aircraft’s rear crew door and barricaded himself inside using an assortment of supplies and tools he had brought with him, a portion of which are pictured below: O’CORRAIN then proceeded to inflict severe damage to the interior of the Aircraft by, among other things, cutting wire bundles and hydraulic lines within the Aircraft, crimping a liquid oxygen line within the Aircraft, destroying every gauge in the Aircraft’s cockpit, and puncturing the Aircraft’s air ducts. Pictured below are examples of the damage inflicted by O’CORRAIN to the interior of the Aircraft: O’CORRAIN also brought multiple capsules of gallium—a highly corrosive metal that is a liquid at room temperature, and which eats through aluminum in minutes and causes long-term corrosion to steel—onto the Aircraft, which is constructed substantially of aluminum. Several hours after O’CORRAIN first entered the airport, the Aircraft’s flight crew (the “Crew”) returned to the Aircraft to depart for their next destination, observed O’CORRAIN through a cockpit window, and notified Shannon Airport security. Members of the Crew then observed O’CORRAIN escape out of a hatch in the Aircraft’s roof and inflict substantial additional damage to the Aircraft’s exterior, including by striking the exterior of the Aircraft with an axe, and pouring unknown substances and placing objects, including ball bearings, into the Aircraft’s fuel tanks. Pictured below is an example of the damage inflicted by O’CORRAIN to the exterior of the Aircraft: Irish law enforcement authorities arrived at the scene shortly thereafter and apprehended O’CORRAIN. Pictured below is O’CORRAIN on the roof of the Aircraft, prior to being apprehended: O’CORRAIN carried out the attack after months of planning and preparation. Among other things, O’CORRAIN, in advance of his attack, conducted online searches regarding the Aircraft’s construction, and later that same day, ordered gallium from an online distributor; acquired an assortment of tools and equipment used in the attack; searched online for coordinates and locations relevant to his attack, including coordinates for where to breach Shannon Airport’s security perimeter; subscribed to a mobile application that tracks the movements of aircraft (including military aircraft); conducted research concerning prior attacks on U.S. military aircraft at Shannon Airport; and attempted to contact an individual involved in one such prior attack. The manner in which O’CORRAIN carried out his attack further demonstrated a detailed knowledge of, among other things, the layout of C-130H aircraft and how best to destroy critical components of the Aircraft; which wires and components to cut and which not to cut, for his own personal safety; how to secure points of entry into the Aircraft, and what tools would be needed to do so; which chemicals, including gallium, could be used to corrode the Aircraft’s primary material; and advanced knowledge that a U.S. military C-130H aircraft would be located at Shannon Airport at the time of his attack. Notably, had O’CORRAIN cut, rather than crimped, the Aircraft’s liquid oxygen line, as he had its wire bundles, there would have been a high chance of a massive explosion within the Aircraft. As a result of O’CORRAIN’s attack, the Aircraft was effectively destroyed. The damage inflicted rendered the Aircraft inoperable, and the Aircraft—worth approximately $60 million—will not return to active flight status. O’CORRAIN’s attack followed a series of similar, though less serious, incidents carried out by others at Shannon Airport over the preceding year. Specifically, on or about May 1, 2025, three individuals were arrested by Irish authorities after driving a van through the Shannon Airport perimeter fence; on or about May 17, 2025, three individuals breached the runway at Shannon Airport and sprayed a U.S. military aircraft with paint, temporarily rendering it inoperable; and on or about November 22, 2025, three individuals breached Shannon Airport’s security perimeter in a van and drove to a restricted area where a U.S. military C-40 aircraft was parked, before being intercepted and detained by airport security. *                *                * O’CORRAIN, 48, of Ireland, is charged with destruction of government property, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison. The maximum potential sentence in this case is prescribed by Congress and provided here for informational purposes only, as any sentencing of the defendant will be determined by the judge. Mr. McDonald praised the outstanding efforts of the FBI’s New York Joint Terrorism Task Force, which consists of investigators and analysts from the FBI, the New York City Police Department, and over 50 other federal, state, and local agencies, as well as the FBI’s Law Enforcement Attaché Office in London. Mr. McDonald also praised the significant assistance provided by the Department of Justice’s National Security Division, Counterterrorism Section; the Department of Justice’s Office of International Affairs; the United States Air Force’s Office of Special Investigations; the Missouri Air National Guard; and the Government of Ireland. This prosecution is being handled by the Office’s National Security and International Narcotics Unit. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jonathan L. Bodansky and Adam Z. Margulies are in charge of the prosecution. The charges contained in the Indictment are merely accusations, and the defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. ^ As the introductory phrase signifies, the entirety of the text of the Indictment and the description of the Indictment set forth herein constitute only allegations, and every fact described therein should be treated as an allegation. title: U.S. Attorney’s Office’s Collection and Enforcement Efforts Net Nearly $80 Million in Fiscal Year 2026
JOINT STATEMENT FROM DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE AND DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE ON MEGASPEED INVESTIGATION
body: Press Release JOINT STATEMENT FROM DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE AND DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE ON MEGASPEED INVESTIGATION Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs OAG The Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice are providing the public with an update on the investigation of the Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has attracted significant public attention in the last week.  While we don’t typically comment on ongoing investigations, it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting. After identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion, the Department of Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations.  In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed.  In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list.  Based on the Department of Commerce’s investigation, agents from the Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang. Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed. The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred.  This investigation is the result of the excellent work of the Department of Commerce under Secretary Howard Lutnick and the law enforcement efforts of the Department of Justice under Attorney General Todd Blanche. The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce have an extremely strong track record of bringing semiconductor smugglers to justice.  Under the Trump Administration, seventeen defendants across six separate investigations have been charged in connection with allegations of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of semiconductors.  Furthermore, the Department of Commerce has brought monetary penalties to new highs across export control cases, representing an eighteen-fold increase over the Biden administration. Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the U.S. economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursing justice for those who want to compromise America’s technological edge. View Joint Statement Here Updated November 17, 2026 Component Office of the Attorney General Press Release Number: 26-1365

Tajik National Convicted of Providing Material Support to ISIS and Firearms Offenses
body: Press Release Tajik National Convicted of Providing Material Support to ISIS and Firearms Offenses Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of New York The Defendant Sent Tens of Thousands of Dollars to ISIS Members Overseas, Used a Sham Marriage to Try to Obtain Status,  and Illegally Possessed Firearms and Ammunition BROOKLYN, NY –  A federal jury in Brooklyn today convicted Mansuri Manuchekhri, also known as “Mansuri Manchekhri” and “Manysher,” on all four counts of an indictment charging him with conspiring to provide material support to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham and the Islamic State-Khorasan Province (ISIS-K), conspiring to possess and possessing firearms and ammunition while unlawfully in the United States, and making false statements to federal agents.  The verdict was returned following a one-week trial before United States District Judge Hector Gonzalez.  Previously, on October 30, 2026, Manuchekhri pleaded guilty to immigration fraud relating to a sham marriage between him and a U.S. citizen. When sentenced on all those crimes, the defendant faces up to 55 years in prison. Joseph Nocella, Jr., United States Attorney for the Eastern District of New York; M. Scott Proctor, Acting Assistant Attorney General for the Justice Department’s National Security Division; James C. Barnacle, Jr., Assistant Director in Charge, Federal Bureau of Investigation, New York Field Office (FBI); and Jessica S. Tisch, Commissioner, New York City Police Department (NYPD), announced the verdict. “The defendant sent money to ISIS, a bloodthirsty terrorist organization, while training with assault rifles and proclaiming to his associates: ‘I am ready,’” stated United States Attorney Nocella.  “But it is we who were ready, along with our law enforcement partners.  The defendant’s conviction has neutralized a serious threat and shown the world that we will be unrelenting in dismantling terrorist funding networks.” Mr. Nocella thanked the FBI’s New York Joint Terrorism Task Force, which consists of investigators and analysts from the FBI, the NYPD and over 50 other federal, state and local agencies, for their outstanding work on the case. “Manuchekhri is a dangerous illegal alien who glorified ISIS’s violence, facilitated payments to ISIS-linked operatives, and unlawfully possessed firearms while living in the United States,” said Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General Proctor.  “His support for a terrorist organization responsible for murder and atrocities around the world, disregard for our nation’s laws, and obvious hatred of the United States made him a grave danger to the public.  Today’s verdict demonstrates that those who aid terrorists will be held fully accountable.” “Mansuri Manuchekhri's alleged extremist plans were disrupted by the outstanding work of the New York Joint Terrorism Force.  He spent years living in New York while supporting ISIS and declaring his allegiance to the group.  Today, he is off the streets.  Anyone who seeks to support or commit terrorism should know that justice will find you,” stated FBI Assistant Director in Charge Barnacle. “Mansuri Manuchekhri sent money overseas to members of ISIS to support acts of terrorism and also amassed an illegal collection of guns here in New York City,” stated NYPD Commissioner Tisch.  “This case is yet another example of the importance and reach of the NYPD’s counterterrorism and intelligence work — Manuchekhri’s preparations could have resulted in mass violence, but our investigation identified the threat, stopped this flow of international funding, and prevented harm from coming to our communities.  I thank our NYPD investigators, law enforcement partners, and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of New York for their continued commitment to fighting global terror.” As proved at trial, in June 2016, the defendant traveled to the United States from Tajikistan on a non-immigrant tourist visa and unlawfully remained in the United States after his visa expired in December 2016.  While in the United States, the defendant collected jihadist propaganda videos that promoted violence and martyrdom and expressed his support for ISIS, praising past ISIS attacks in the United States such as the October 2017 West Side Highway truck attack that killed eight people.  The defendant’s ex-wife testified that he told her about the terrorist who carried out that deadly attack: “That guy is in heaven.” From approximately December 2021 through June 2023, while residing in Brooklyn, the defendant facilitated approximately $70,000 in payments to ISIS-affiliated co-conspirators in Türkiye and Syria, including to an individual who was later arrested by Turkish authorities for his alleged involvement in a January 2024 terrorist attack on a church in Istanbul for which ISIS-K publicly claimed responsibility.  In March 2017, the defendant paid an American citizen to enter into a sham marriage with him so that he could obtain legal status in the United States.  However, he failed to provide certain supporting documentation that was requested by the government, and his petition was never granted. Within the same time frame as the money transfers to ISIS, the defendant possessed and used firearms and made frequent visits to shooting ranges even though he was prohibited from doing so as an alien unlawfully in the United States.  In February 2022, the defendant recorded himself firing an assault rifle at a shooting range in New Jersey and sent the video to one of the ISIS-affiliated individuals in Türkiye with the message, “Thank God, I am ready, brother.”  An invoice from the shooting range reflects that on February 27, 2022, the defendant and his friend rented a rifle port, an AK-47, and a Smith & Wesson M&P 15 tactical rifle, and purchased ammunition. The defendant also possessed firearms elsewhere.  On August 24, 2024, the defendant sent a different roommate a video recorded from inside a moving vehicle showing the defendant’s outstretched arm firing a handgun out the window along a highway. The government’s case is being handled by the Office’s National Security and Cybercrime Section.  Assistant United States Attorneys Andrew D. Reich and Lindsey R. Oken are in charge of the prosecution, with valuable assistance from Assistant United States Attorney Robert Pollack, Dylan Stern, and Andrew Stamboulidis; Trial Attorney John Cella and Ryan White of the Department’s National Security Division, Counterterrorism Section; and Paralegal Specialist Wayne H. Colon. The Defendant : MANSURI MANUCHEKHRI (also known as “Mansuri Manchekhri” and “Manysher”) Age: 35 Brooklyn, New York E.D.N.Y. title: Previously convicted felon pleads guilty to federal gun crime as part of ‘Operation Fly City’
body: Press Release Previously convicted felon pleads guilty to federal gun crime as part of ‘Operation Fly City’ Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of Ohio DAYTON, Ohio – Another of the 47 defendants charged this summer as part of the “Operation Fly City” Homeland Security Task Force enforcement surge pleaded guilty in U.S. District Court today to a federal firearms crime. Marlin Robinson, 33, of Cincinnati, appeared in federal court in Dayton today to enter his guilty plea. According to court documents, Robinson possessed a 9mm pistol on May 28. As a previously convicted felon, he is prohibited from possessing firearms or ammunition. Robinson’s criminal history includes multiple convictions for heroin trafficking in both Greene and Scioto counties. Possessing a firearm or ammunition as a previously convicted felon is a federal crime punishable by up to 15 years in prison.  Sentencing of the defendant will be determined by the Court based on the advisory sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors at a future hearing. Dominick S. Gerace II, United States Attorney for the Southern District of Ohio; Jorge Rosendo, Special Agent in Charge, U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms & Explosives (ATF); Michael Larson, Acting Special Agent in Charge, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit; Dayton Police Chief Eric Henderson; and Montgomery County Sheriff Rob Streck; announced the guilty plea offered before U.S. Magistrate Judge Peter B. Silvain, Jr. Assistant United States Attorneys Sabrina A. Montgomery and Rob Painter are representing the United States in this case. These cases are part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Cincinnati comprises agents and officers from federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies. # # # Updated November 17, 2026 Topics Firearms Offenses Violent Crime Component USAO - Ohio, Southern

title: PACE Organization InnovAge Agrees to Pay $36M to Resolve False Claims Act Allegations of Failing to Provide Comprehensive Medical Services and Timely Specialist Referrals to Seniors
body: Press Release PACE Organization InnovAge Agrees to Pay $36M to Resolve False Claims Act Allegations of Failing to Provide Comprehensive Medical Services and Timely Specialist Referrals to Seniors Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Colorado USACO.PublicAffairs@usdoj.gov DENVER - InnovAge Holding Corporation (InnovAge), headquartered in Denver, Colorado, has agreed to pay a total of $36 million to resolve allegations that it violated the federal False Claims Act and state laws by failing to provide required comprehensive medical services and timely referrals to medical specialists as expeditiously as its patients’ health conditions required. “Failing to provide comprehensive medical services and timely specialist referrals threatens the health of our most vulnerable seniors,” said Acting Assistant Attorney General Jonathan D. Guynn of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “This historic, first-of-its-kind settlement demonstrates the Civil Division’s commitment to combating healthcare fraud by PACE organizations.” “Elderly patients suffer when PACE providers like InnovAge do not fulfill their obligations to schedule patient visits with medical specialists in a timely manner,” said U.S. Attorney Peter McNeilly for the District of Colorado. “The U.S. Attorney’s Office in Colorado is committed to holding PACE providers accountable to ensure they provide comprehensive and timely care.” “PACE organizations that receive Medicare and Medicaid funding must meet their obligations to provide timely and comprehensive care to the vulnerable seniors they serve as delays can jeopardize the health of patients,” said Acting Deputy Inspector General for Investigations Miranda L. Bennett of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG). “This settlement demonstrates that organizations that fail to comply with those requirements will be held accountable. HHS-OIG remains committed to working with our law enforcement partners and leveraging the False Claims Act to help ensure providers comply with program requirements and deliver the care their patients need.” InnovAge provides services to seniors under a dual Medicare-Medicaid program called the Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE). InnovAge has PACE centers in several states, including California, Colorado, New Mexico, and the Commonwealth of Virginia. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) pays PACE organizations a fixed monthly amount for each Medicare beneficiary enrolled in their programs. In return, PACE organizations must provide comprehensive health care services to their participants, and all services must be provided as expeditiously as the participant’s health condition requires. This settlement resolves allegations that, from May 2016 to October 2022, InnovAge failed to provide comprehensive health care services as expeditiously as required by its patients. Specifically, InnovAge allegedly failed to maintain sufficient specialist provider networks and, in thousands of instances, InnovAge failed to timely schedule appointments or consultations for specialist medical care, such as for oncology, cardiology, surgery, and neurology, for its patients. The United States and various states further alleged that InnovAge’s internal reports of providers’ medical orders regularly showed numerous and recurrent delinquent specialist referrals. Several senior InnovAge physicians also complained to InnovAge about the company’s scheduling practices and delays for specialist referrals. These complaints included that InnovAge’s scheduling practices and delays had negative health care consequences for participants, placed legal risk on InnovAge’s healthcare providers, and put InnovAge out of compliance with CMS requirements. In addition, InnovAge’s internal audits found significant delays in specialist care, including numerous delayed orders, of which many were over a year outstanding. As a result of this settlement, InnovAge will pay approximately $25.7 million to the United States and a combined $10.3 million to the States of Colorado, California, and New Mexico, and the Commonwealth of Virginia. The civil settlement includes the resolution of federal and states’ claims brought under the qui tam or whistleblower provisions of the False Claims Act and analogous state statutes by two former employees, Monita Poudyal and Karen Lapcewich. Under those provisions, a private party can file an action on behalf of the United States and receive a portion of any recovery. The qui tam cases are captioned United States ex rel. Poudyal v. InnovAge Holding Corp., et al. , No. 1:21-cv-02464 (D. Colo.) and United States ex rel. Lapcewich v. Total Community Options Inc., et al. , No. 1:22-cv-01686 (D. Colo.). The relator share of the federal settlement will be $4.5 million. This year the Administration launched the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud and the National Fraud Enforcement Division to enhance the Administration’s war on fraud, waste, and abuse in federal programs. When unscrupulous actors exploit these programs for their own financial gain, they defraud the government, harm the people these programs are designed to aid and protect, and undermine American businesses that play by the rules. The Civil Division’s FCA enforcement plays a critical role in combatting such fraudulent schemes, recovering billions of dollars for the American taxpayers, and holding wrongdoers accountable. FCA matters will continue to be on the forefront of the battle against fraud, and the Civil Division’s FCA work will support and advance the mission of the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud and the National Fraud Enforcement Division. The resolution obtained in this matter was the result of a coordinated effort between the Justice Department’s Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section, and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Colorado, with assistance from the Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General. The investigation and resolution of this matter illustrates the government’s emphasis on combating healthcare fraud. One of the most powerful tools in this effort is the False Claims Act. Tips and complaints from all sources about potential fraud, waste, abuse, and mismanagement, can be reported to the Department of Health and Human Services at 800-HHS-TIPS (800-447-8477). Trial Attorneys Yifan Wang and David G. Miller of the Civil Division and Assistant U.S. Attorney Lila Bateman for the District of Colorado handled the matter. The claims resolved by the settlement are allegations only and there has been no determination of liability. Contact USACO.PublicAffairs@usdoj.gov Updated November 17, 2026 Component USAO - Colorado

title: New Orleans Man and Texas Woman Plead Guilty to Conspiracy to Commit Wire Fraud and a Violation of the Federal Controlled Substances Act
body: Press Release New Orleans Man and Texas Woman Plead Guilty to Conspiracy to Commit Wire Fraud and a Violation of the Federal Controlled Substances Act Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Louisiana shane.jones@usdoj.gov NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA – KEVIN J. THOMPSON , age 41, a resident of New Orleans, and NINA THOMAS , age 37, a resident of Austin, Texas, pled guilty on November 12, 2026, before United States District Judge Brandon S. Long to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, in violation of Title 18, United States Code, Sections 1343 and 371, announced U.S. Attorney David I. Courcelle. THOMPSON also pled guilty to possession with intent to distribute five hundred grams or more of cocaine, in violation of (a)(1), 841(b)(1)(B). According to court documents, in December 2020, THOMAS filed a petition for divorce from her husband, (“the victim”) who is under a guardianship because of his mental incapacity.  Under the terms of a court order, both parties were ordered to not transfer property or negotiate any negotiable instruments or checks in the other’s name. In 2021, THOMAS entered into a romantic relationship with THOMPSON . THOMAS and THOMPSON then devised a scheme with the intent to defraud the victim of money and property by way of false material representations, including by impersonating the victim and making unauthorized financial transfers by electronic wires.  As part of their scheme, in 2022, THOMAS and THOMPSON opened accounts at a credit union and bank in the Eastern District of Louisiana under the victim’s name. At the direction of THOMAS , THOMPSON practiced signing the victim’s name.  After the accounts were opened, a direct deposit authorization form was signed and submitted to the victim’s labor union association, directing all payments for the victim to be deposited into the bank account without the victim’s authorization.  One check deposited into the account totaled $885,419.00.  On several occasions between 2022 and 2023, THOMPSON , using the victim’s identification and aided by THOMAS , deposited or withdrew hundreds of thousands of dollars from a bank in New Orleans.  The deposits included checks from the labor union association payable to the victim along with proceeds from vehicles owned by the victim that were sold without his authorization.  Also, THOMAS and THOMPSON used the victim’s driver’s license to complete a third-party credit card authorization debiting the victim’s credit card for plastic surgery for another individual.  Proceeds from some of the other transactions were used to purchase luxury items for THOMAS and THOMPSON .  In total, THOMAS and THOMSPON stole between $1,500,000.00 and $3,000,000.00 from the victim. In June 2023, the credit union contacted the Jefferson Parish Sheriff’s Office and informed them that an individual had assumed the victim’s identity and had withdrawn more than $700,000.00 from the victim’s account. THOMPSON , who was scheduled to visit the credit union, arrived driving a Rolls Royce fraudulently obtained from the victim.  Credit union officials reviewed the membership form and learned that though the account was in the victim’s name, the phone number used to open the account was THOMPSON’s .  Officers arrested THOMPSON who was in possession of a driver’s license, social security card and bank cards in the victim’s name.  Officers obtained a search warrant for THOMPSON’s residence and seized 3,716 grams of cocaine, a Springfield Armory HS Produkt Hellcat pistol and $228,000.00 cash. On the wire fraud conspiracy count, THOMAS and THOMPSON each face a maximum term of imprisonment of five (5) years, a fine of up to $250,000.00, up to three (3) years of supervised release following any term of imprisonment and a mandatory special assessment fee of $100.00. On the drug count THOMPSON faces a minimum term of imprisonment of five (5) years, a maximum term of imprisonment of forty (40) years, a fine of up to $5,000,000.00, at least four (4) years of supervised release following any term of imprisonment and a mandatory special assessment fee of $100.00. The case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the Jefferson Parish Sheriff’s Office.  The prosecution is being handled by Assistant United States Attorney André Jones of the Narcotics Unit. *       *        * Contact Shane M. Jones Public Information Officer United States Attorney’s Office, Eastern District of Louisiana United States Department of Justice Updated November 17, 2026 Topics Fraud Identity Theft Components Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) USAO - Louisiana, Eastern

title: Extradited Mexican National Pleads Guilty to Fentanyl Trafficking in Homeland Security Task Force Investigation
body: Press Release Extradited Mexican National Pleads Guilty to Fentanyl Trafficking in Homeland Security Task Force Investigation Tuesday, November 17, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of California Kelly.Thornton@usdoj.gov SAN DIEGO – An extradited Mexican national pleaded guilty in federal court today to conspiring to import massive quantities of fentanyl into the United States. According to court documents, Fausto Ramirez, 71, was a leader of a network that imported over 450,000 counterfeit, fentanyl-laced “M-30s” into the United States through the San Ysidro and Nogales Ports of Entry. Ramirez’s network of couriers brought in these pills which were then supplied to distributors across San Diego County and the United States. This long-term investigation linked Ramirez and his network to distributors who sold thousands of fentanyl pills on “Dream Market,” a dark web marketplace where users buy and sell illegal substances and services. Ramirez was arrested in Tijuana, Mexico on August 8, 2025, at the request of the United States and was extradited to the United States on December 10, 2025. He is scheduled to be sentenced on February 12, 2027 before U.S. District Judge Janis L. Sammartino. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs, the U.S. Department of State, and the U.S. Embassy in Mexico provided significant assistance in securing the defendant’s arrest and extradition from Mexico. The U.S. Marshals Service assisted in bringing the defendant to the United States. This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew J. Sutton. DEFENDANT Case Number 23-cr-01575-JLS Fausto Ramirez                                               Age: 71                                   Tijuana, MX SUMMARY OF CHARGES Conspiracy to Import Fentanyl, in violation of Title 21 U.S.C. §§ 952, 960 and 963. Maximum Penalty: Mandatory minimum 10 years and up to life in prison, $10 million fine. INVESTIGATING AGENCY Homeland Security Investigations Drug Enforcement Administration United States Postal Inspection Service United States Marshals Service This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF San Diego comprises agents and officers from FBI, Homeland Security Investigations, DEA, ATF, U.S. Marshals, Department of Defense, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, Naval Criminal Investigative Service, IRS Criminal Investigation, U.S. Coast Guard, U.S. Customs and Border Protection and Interpol, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of California. Updated November 17, 2026 Topics Drug Trafficking Opioids Component USAO - California, Southern Press Release Number: CAS26-1117-Ramirez

title: NVIDIA DGX Spark Developer Kit Turns a Desk Into a Supercomputing Lab
body: NVIDIA DGX Spark Developer Kit Turns a Desk Into a Supercomputing Lab November 16, 2026 by Allen Bourgoyne 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers. The kit is a four-node cluster of NVIDIA DGX Spark systems , each connected directly to its two neighbors in a ring, with an NVIDIA HPC SDK installation playbook coming soon. Researchers get a place at their desk to run multi-node scientific workloads, AI models and agents, instead of waiting for time on a shared GPU cluster. The kit puts the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip on researchers’ desks. A Supercomputing Lab on Any Desk The DGX Spark Developer Kit changes how researchers work. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up. At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 20TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1. With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises. The playbook for NVIDIA HPC SDK is coming soon, bringing GPU-accelerated C, C++ and Fortran compilers, libraries and message passing interface tools to the DGX Spark cluster — the same development tools used on NVIDIA-powered supercomputers. Teams can build and test scientific applications across four nodes, check how computation and data are distributed, and debug communication issues before scaling to larger systems. The kit brings scientific simulation and AI models and agents to the desktop, with demonstrated four-system workloads including LAMMPS with Kokkos for materials simulation and NAMD for molecular dynamics. The broader DGX Spark community has validated GROMACS for molecular dynamics, OpenFOAM for fluid dynamics, WRF for weather modeling and NVIDIA NIM microservices such as OpenFold3 and Boltz-2 for predicting biomolecular structures. Running on DGX Spark, new open dataset and post-training recipes for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL help researchers adapt the model for life sciences and chemistry, enabling secure scientific workflows on infrastructure organizations control. What Researchers Can Do With It The kit opens up new possibilities for researchers. Researchers can explore agent-assisted workflows that prepare simulation inputs, launch runs and summarize results, while the scientists validate the setup and conclusions. Researchers can also train AI models that approximate slow simulations, then use them to refine wing designs toward minimum drag. Before committing supercomputer time, a team can narrow a 10-million-cell simulation to the 50-500 dimensions that matter. Kvantify is using NVIDIA cuQuantum, and reports running tensor-network simulations of quantum-chemistry circuits with up to 70 qubits and 975 gates on a single DGX Spark, benchmarking circuits generated for penicillin ground-state energy calculations. CYRAN AI , an IIT Delhi spin-out, uses DGX Spark and its PixelFlux library to accelerate JPEG 2000 decoding for large satellite images, supporting local geospatial analysis. OpenFold shows how researchers can fine-tune OpenFold3 on NVIDIA DGX Spark to improve protein-ligand structure predictions for drug discovery. The Rubin Lab at IGI at University of California, Berkeley is using a DGX Spark and NVIDIA Evo 2 model to predict bacterial traits directly from genome sequences by comparing embeddings from genomic and protein language models against the classical baselines. With no 11-hour cluster queue times, results arrived 15x sooner on DGX Spark. The Hartwig Group at UC Berkeley is using a DGX Spark to perform LoRA fine-tuning on the Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B model for chemistry machine learning, training a prediction head on experimental values. By running locally on the Spark using NVFP4 quantization, the lab successfully fit a 120B-class model on a single device and bypassed multi-day cluster queue times, allowing them to run continuous eight- to 24-hour training fits back-to-back. Where to Find the Kit The developer kit is on display at SC26 and available for sale. DGX Spark products and cables can be purchased from top OEM partners and are also available through NVIDIA Marketplace . Partners include Acer, ASUS, Dell Technologies, GIGABYTE, H3C, HP, Lenovo, MSI and xFusion. An NVIDIA playbook for building and running the NVIDIA HPC SDK, a software development kit for scientific computing, is coming soon. Once available, it will give scientists and researchers a local platform to develop multi-node GPU applications, explore FP32 and mixed-precision algorithms and run molecular dynamics and materials simulations using LAMMPS with Kokkos before scaling to data center systems. Learn more about NVIDIA DGX Spark . Subscribe to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter . Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X , Instagram , TikTok and Facebook . See notice regarding software product information. title: How the World’s Most Advanced AI Infrastructure Supply Chain Invents the Future
body: How the World’s Most Advanced AI Infrastructure Supply Chain Invents the Future Over two decades running the most complex manufacturing on the planet, NVIDIA operations chief Deb Shoquist has required three things of every supply chain partner: extreme technical skill, unshakeable trust and a willingness to always try something new. November 16, 2026 by NVIDIA Writers 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Deb Shoquist leads operations at NVIDIA, overseeing the supply chain and manufacturing behind its AI platforms. That description sums up the job, but it doesn’t begin to encompass what Shoquist has made possible over decades. Shoquist, her team and their global network of manufacturing partners enable NVIDIA to introduce world-leading technologies year-round. Much of the team’s success comes down to her deep relationships with some of the world’s most accomplished manufacturers, including TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron, SPIL, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Unimicron, Lumentum, Coherent and Amkor. TSMC has partnered with NVIDIA since 1998. SPIL and KYEC were assembling and testing its chips more than two decades ago. For Shoquist, those relationships grow stronger through each challenge solved together on the factory floor, as every generation of technology demands more from the people and tools behind it. Ask her about the global network she relies on, and she starts with the people. There’s the supplier in Taiwan so eager to get production moving that he calls her at 3 a.m. with a fix to the latest problem. There are the factory workers in Vietnam whose only ask of her are more tools to get more work done. She remembers the partners that supported NVIDIA when it was small, and the work they’ve done to help each other grow. Shoquist meets with key suppliers quarterly and spends six weeks each year on the road visiting partners in Taiwan, China, Korea, Vietnam and the U.S., where conversations move from meeting rooms to factory floors. Recently, she paused her travels to accept the 2026 Dr. Lisa Su Woman of Innovation Award — and to share how she finds the right people and companies to imagine and produce at massive scale technology that has never been built before. Foxconn Q: How would you describe your job to someone outside NVIDIA? A: At the most basic level, our job is to convert designs into the physical world. Our design team creates a blueprint, and our job is to transition it into a reliable, high-performance supply chain. A matchmaker is probably the best analogy. You have to find the partner that matches your ramp style and has the technology that can meet the needs of very precise designs. The supplier has to be financially strong enough to invest in our ramps. They have to be highly technical. And they have to be willing to do something that has never been done before. If you don’t have all three, you can’t create products at the volume and speed that we need. You need those three legs, and in some cases, if you only have two, you have to invest in the company to make them a partner. Q: What’s an example of that in practice ? A: Amphenol’s cable cartridge is the most complex interconnect assembly they have ever built. When I recently visited the Vietnam factory, now in full production, I was struck by the level of precision required to build a product of this complexity. In this large cable cartridge, there are 1,500 small cable legs. Each one requires a very precise assembly to yield a quality level of less than 1 DPPM, or defect part per million. Amphenol built over a hundred automated lines to produce this product at the speed and scale we require. That takes know-how and technology, but it also takes heart, willingness and dedication. Creating anything of that complexity and precision with a supplier forges the partnership. The partners NVIDIA maintains are the ones who supported us when we were small, and yet are willing to scale with us today. Q: What changed as NVIDIA went from selling chips to building systems and platforms? A: When we were primarily a chip manufacturer, we were small, and the semiconductor industry was at scale. In that environment, it was about picking the best technology match for the products we envisioned. As we became a data center systems company, we needed more partners. But we’ve also now entered into new technology areas where the scale of the supply base is still developing. For example, our optical component partners have the technology and the willingness, but they don’t yet have the scale or capital to build fabs for the volume we need. To grow, we needed to support and invest, like we did with Coherent and Lumentum . Beyond that, with products like CPO (co-packaged optics), we’re creating entirely new supply chains with scale partners that are new to the optics world. Leading the integration of talent across the supply chain is the key to driving this incredible technology to high volume quickly. Wistron Q: You clearly enjoy spending time with supply partners, and in particular on the factory floor. What have you learned there over time that can’t be learned anywhere else? A: Over 20 years, you meet many individuals key to the success of your supply. You meet not only the CEOs, but also the people that are running the production floor. These are the people that really know the problems of manufacturing. If you don’t have a tight working relationship with the people deeper in the organization, then it’s hard to have an open dialogue about any challenges. But when you have tight relationships, they want to help you, and they feel comfortable enough telling you, “I need better technical support on the floor. I need more quality engineers. We need a better design. We need to automate this. We need more buffers of material.” That’s what 20 years of working with our suppliers has taught us. It’s year after year of learning from people, getting to know people deeper in the organization and creating the trust where they can tell us what we need to do to be successful with them. Q: Demand for NVIDIA technology is already massive and growing. Your job is to make sure NVIDIA’s volume can keep up. How do you make it happen? A: It goes back to relationships. When you decide that you’re going to push a line hard to increase volume, you have to have the relationships. You have to know their processes in detail. You have to know their people in detail, and they have to trust you. Only then are you in a position to ask them for special favors, because you can do it surgically, and your ask is credible and reasonable. And when you’re successful together, they’re happy, you’re happy, and the appreciation for the partnership deepens. We all appreciate those that make us successful. Coherent Q: How do you prioritize resources across the supply chain? A: You need to first understand what the most critical components are, and protect and prioritize production around them. We need wafers like we need air. And the critical component is the TSMC chip. As it comes out of assembly every week, we decide what factory gets what chip. Every week, we look at factory performance. If a particular factory yield is low, if their time of ownership is not at the level we want, they don’t get more chips that week. We keep track of every chip, from the identification number on the die all the way to the customer invoice. If you want to be our supplier, you have to support that traceability process. With that process, we took the time it takes from chip out at TSMC to system out at Foxconn and Wistron from five to two weeks when supply and demand requires it. Think of the supply chain as a large circulatory system with pathways everywhere — and when you need to accelerate any branch of it, you have the power to do that. We have the capability to do that. It’s empowering and exciting. Amphenol Q: What’s an example of a time things didn’t go as planned? How did you, the team and your partners find a way forward? A: We were getting ready to go to volume production with Foxconn and Wistron for the compute board of NVIDIA GB200 . The last step in the process was a test managed by an automated handler — a completely new approach for us, developed to meet the demands of high-volume throughput for these complicated products. During the initial ramp, the throughput was significantly below plan. The operations director of Taiwan manufacturing made the call that to protect the product and shipments, he needed to disable the entire process and return to manual test loading. Our manufacturers backed him without question and brought in the necessary manpower to meet the immediate needs, literally hundreds of operators. That kept production moving, but would not solve the throughput requirement of full production. As with any operations problem, the root cause had many elements to it: test tray assembly, test tray design, automation hardware design, automation control software, product yield. From all viewpoints, it was a difficult problem to resolve quickly. That’s when we executed the NVIDIA swarm. Teams from NVIDIA design engineering, operations industrial, and product and test engineering, as well as from Foxconn automation engineering, flooded the line with talent to redesign and reactivate the line before the scale ramp hit. This is not an unusual occurrence when there is a problem in operations. All teams at NVIDIA are street fighters — action-oriented, and know no organizational boundaries. We say that “the mission is the boss,” but we also live “the mission is the boss.” Q: What makes this work so exciting for you? A: Operations is a very empowering place to be at NVIDIA. Our team is designing and implementing changes to the supply chain constantly to meet the strong demand of our new products. The challenges are understandably high, but we’re always given the resources we need to be successful. The only thing between our goals and our success is our own creativity. That is exhilarating.
